items.title: KP police put on alert as emergency ‘looms’
items.description: PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed on Saturday put district police on alert for possible violent protests and sabotage in the event of the federal government imposing an emergency in the province, emphasising caution in the use of force. A notification issued by the IGP’s office outlined guidelines for handling protests and warned that miscreants and anti-state elements could exploit demonstrations to incite violence and carry out sabotage activities. “To protect lives and property and prevent sabotage during protests, DPOs, sub-divisional police officers and station house officers should personally monitor all protests within their respective jurisdictions,” it said. The notification said district police must ensure that sufficient personnel were made available to SDPOs and SHOs to maintain order during protests. “The deployment should include anti-riot squads equipped with anti-riot gear, an adequate supply of gas guns and shells checked and verified for use by reserve inspectors or moharrars, special squads of unarmed personnel to identify and apprehend troublemakers and violent protesters, and plainclothes personnel deployed to identify violent protesters, troublemakers and saboteurs. Armed personnel should be deployed only at important or suitable points in extremely urgent situations.” IGP issues guidelines for handling violent protests, stresses caution in use of force The police chief directed SHOs to identify vulnerable locations along protest routes and deploy sufficient personnel to protect them. “Such places may include police stations and police offices, government buildings, petrol stations, banks, shopping centres, important highways/roads and any other sensitive installations,” the notification said. The notification said DPOs could require protest organisers to obtain a licence for an assembly or protest under Section 84 of the KP Police Act, 2017, or any other law or regulation in force, if they considered a breach of the peace likely. According to the guidelines, a DPO, SDPO or SHO could stop a procession that violated the conditions of a licence granted under Section 84 of the KP Police Act, 2017, and order it or any assembly violating such conditions to disperse. “Any procession or assembly, which neglects or refuses to obey any order given Under-Section 85 Sub-Section (I) of Police Act, 2017 or any other law in force shall be deemed an unlawful assembly.” The notification said DPOs could issue appropriate directions, instructions or guidelines to regulate protests and ensure public safety. In the event of violence, they could also take necessary legal action. It added that any police officer could temporarily close or regulate a street or public place by erecting barriers or using other means to prevent people or vehicles from entering an area for security reasons, as provided under Section 88 of the KP Police Act, 2017. According to the notification, during peaceful protests and roadblocks, police should exercise maximum restraint and avoid using force. Protesters should be engaged in negotiations by the senior-most police officer available at the scene, who should try to persuade them to disperse peacefully. It said to prevent serious disorder, a breach of law or imminent danger to life and property, SDPOs, SHOs or the senior-most officer present at the scene could order the appropriate use of force after assessing the situation and declaring the assembly unlawful. The notification said the senior-most supervisory police officer during protests would determine the type and extent of force to be used to disperse an unlawful assembly. “When it is required to use force as per law, its application shall be of minimum essential standard,” the notification said. It emphasised that the use of force should be graduated, starting at the minimum level and increasing only as necessary. In the first phase, violent protesters should be clearly warned before force was used. According to the notification, if necessary, tear-gas shells or grenades should be used from a safe distance to disperse protesters. Rubber-bullet guns and paper-ball guns could also be used against violent protesters from a safe distance. “In the second phase, if the situation requires, the violent protesters may be stopped with baton charge by using the anti-riot gear. The special unarmed squad will be activated to apprehend the violent protesters and take appropriate legal action,” it said. The notification said in cases of extreme violence and an imminent threat to life and property, aerial firing could be conducted by special armed personnel or squads, but only on the directions of the senior-most officer present at the scene. It added that if a person carried a firearm or any article covered under Section 86(1) of the KP Police Act, 2017, the police could seize it and take legal action against the carrier under Section 148 of the Pakistan Penal Code, the notification said. “Extreme caution shall be used while using the force against protesters to avert damage to life and property. Anti-riot squad or the personnel entrusted with use of force shall be properly equipped with anti-riot gear to avoid damage/casualties to life of all concerned,” it said. The notification said the SHO should arrange video recording of the entire protest or procession, preferably through professional cameramen. In the event of a law and order situation, DPOs should ensure briefings, rehearsals and reporting, and issue instructions strictly in accordance with OG-9/2013. “Prior consultation and coordination should be carried out at all supervisory levels with key stakeholders, including the district administration, law enforcement agencies and other relevant bodies,” it said. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Poverty’s long shadow
items.description: PAKISTAN’S contribution to rising poverty across the Middle East, North Africa and the Afghanistan-Pakistan region is troubling. According to the World Bank, the country accounts for nearly half of the region’s people living in extreme poverty. Ours is a story of repeated hardship. Millions of Pakistanis have endured the pandemic, deadly floods, soaring inflation, and years of economic uncertainty, often with little opportunity to recover before the next crisis arrives. For a poor household, each setback leaves lasting damage. Families may exhaust their savings, sell livestock, borrow money to buy food, or withdraw children from school to save expenses. Even when prices stabilise and incomes improve, the losses are not easily reversed. A farmer who has sold his animals or a small trader who has closed his business cannot simply resume earning a livelihood. This helps explain why poverty can continue to rise even as the wider economy shows signs of recovery. The damage caused by successive crises has accumulated, leaving vulnerable families with fewer resources to withstand another blow. Fresh dangers are emerging. The World Bank has warned that the conflict involving Iran could push up fuel and commodity prices, weaken remittances and increase borrowing costs. Adverse weather could also drive up food prices and hurt agricultural livelihoods. For households still struggling with the effects of earlier shocks, another spell of inflation could prove devastating. The government must, therefore, go beyond providing relief after disaster strikes. It needs to identify families at greatest risk, strengthen early-warning and disaster-response systems, protect farming livelihoods and ensure that financial help reaches vulnerable households before they are forced into desperate choices. Keeping children in school and preventing families from losing their means of earning a living must also be priorities. Poverty reduction cannot succeed if every new crisis pushes people back into hardship. Pakistan must protect the fragile gains its poorest citizens manage to make. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Emergency looms over KP as Centre-PTI rift widens
items.description: • PML-N, PPP leaders finalise plan to bring KP under federal control • PM calls cabinet meeting today to discuss constitutional options • Fazl holds meetings with PM, PTI leaders to defuse tensions • Interior minister says ‘no room left’ to avoid emergency • KP police chief directs security measures ahead of possible protests • Separate NA, Senate sessions to be summoned for Tuesday • Govt plans to invoke various provisions of Articles 232, 233 and 234 ISLAMABAD: As political tensions mounted with the start of the protest march by the opposition PTI, the top leaders of the two major ruling coalition partners — the PML-N and the PPP — on Saturday finalised a plan to bring the troubled Khyber Pakht­unkhwa province under federal control by invoking constitutional provisions regarding imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule, sources close to the development told Dawn. In a related development, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called a meeting of the federal cabinet today (Sunday) to discuss the plan. The ruling coalition leaders also decided to convene separate sessions of the National Assembly and the Senate on Tuesday (Oct 13). The developments followed a flurry of political activities in the federal capital on Saturday, with Prime Minister Shehbaz holding separate meetings with President Asif Zardari and Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman to discuss available options for avoiding a direct confrontation with the opposition PTI, which is in power in KP. The Maulana, who has been playing a role to facilitate the government-opposition talks, also held a meeting with PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and Asad Qaiser and apprised them about the possible government’s move, if the PTI insisted on continuing its march. “We are only facilitators of talks to defuse the prevailing tension but the decision will have to be made by the government and the PTI,” said a senior JUI-F leader after the Maulana’s meeting with the PM and PTI leaders. Though, there were no official words from the government side, the statements issued by a couple of ministers and background interviews with some PPP leaders suggest that the government has made up its mind to invoke various provisions of Articles 232, 233 and 234 of the Constitution to take control of the KP and remove Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi came out more directly when he said, “There was no room left to avoid the imposition of an emergency in KP.” Talking to reporters, Mr Naqvi said the government had made every possible effort but had nothing more to offer [to the PTI]. “Ask Maulana Fazlur Rehman himself how hard I tried,” he said, adding that Barrister Gohar could also be contacted to confirm the efforts he had made in this regard. “I tried my best till the very end, but I have nothing left,” Mr Naqvi added. When contacted, Federal Minister for Information Ataullah Tarar confirmed that the prime minister had convened a meeting of the federal cabinet today (Sunday) to discuss the options of imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. “You can understand the meaning of convening the cabinet meeting on Sunday [a weekly holiday],” the minister said, when asked if the government had decided to impose emergency in KP. Similarly, speaking to a private TV channel, Minister of State for Interior Affairs Tallal Chaudhry also said that multiple options were being examined at different levels but questioned what other avenues were available with the federal government, with the PTI failing to fulfil the federal government’s repeated requests to cooperate in the fight against terrorism, and inciting people and speaking against national policy during the ongoing march. Meanwhile, a senior KP government official told Dawn that all deputy commissioners and district police officers across the province had been directed to remain present in their respective districts till further orders. A source in the federal government has told Dawn that the federal cabinet will approve a slew of measures under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution to proclaim state of an emergency in KP. “A cocktail of the two articles”, as he put it. According to him, the Constitution does not require cabinet approval. “It’s the governor, the president and the prime minister,” he said. The cabinet approval is being done as an additional measure. In another related development, KP Police chief Zulfiqar Hameed on Saturday issued guidelines to all the district police officers in the wake of possible violent protests and sabotage activities in case the federal government announced emergency in the province. “In order to ensure public safety and security, in all cases of public protests there is a possibility that miscreants and anti-state elements may use an opportunity to excite violence, and carry out sabotage activities,” a notification read. The police chief has directed the SHOs to identify vulnerable places falling in the route of the protest procession and deploy sufficient police strength for their protection. The official handout issued by the Presidency after the meeting between the PPP and the PML-N leaders said the prime minister held a meeting with President Asif Zardari and “discussed the overall political and security situation of the country”. The meeting was attended by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, PM’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Attorney General Mansoor Awan and PPP leaders, including Sherry Rehman, Naveed Qamar, Saleem Mandviwala and Dr Asim Hussain. Constitutional provisions Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province. It says, “If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.” However, invoking of this article requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province. “Provided further that if the President acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed before both Houses of Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) for approval by each House within 10 days,” it says. According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency. Article 233 provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during emergency period. On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says. “If the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a Province, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Province cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, the President may, or if a resolution in this behalf is passed by each House separately shall, by Proclamation — (a) assume to himself, or direct the Governor of the Province to assume on behalf of the President, all or any of the functions of the Government of the Province, and all or any of the powers vested in, or exercisable by, anybody or authority in the Province, other than the Provincial Assembly; (b) declare that the powers of the Provincial Assembly shall be exercisable by, or under the authority of, Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament); and (c) make such incidental and consequential provisions as appear to the President to be necessary or desirable for giving effect to the objects of the Proclamation, including provisions for suspending in whole or in part the operation of any provisions of the Constitution relating to any body or authority in the Province,” the article states. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Botched execution survivor in Tennessee, US returns to prison
items.description: WASHINGTON: Convicted murderer Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee last week, has been discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers said on Saturday. Pike, 50, was given two doses of the drug pentobarbital on Sept 30 — a usually fatal dose that nevertheless failed to kill her. She was transported to hospital in critical condition but later regained consciousness, with her lawyers saying this week that she was walking around but in a “foggy” mental state. Pike is the only inmate to ever survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre (DPIC). “Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre where she has been housed for more than 30 years,” her lawyers said in a statement. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” the statement went on. Pike “is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the lawyers said. Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee after she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp. Pike was 18 at the time of the murder. The attempted execution came after days of legal wrangling that ultimately reached the Supreme Court. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Ouagadougou : Poursuivi pour vente de médicaments prohibés, il refuse de révéler les noms de ses fournisseurs
items.description: Issaka (nom d’emprunt), commerçant de 37 ans installé à Ouagadougou, a comparu le lundi 5 octobre 2026 devant la chambre correctionnelle du Tribunal de grande instance Ouaga I. Il est poursuivi pour vente de produits pharmaceutiques prohibés dans le quartier Hamdallaye. Le prévenu a reconnu les faits, mais a refusé de révéler l’identité de ses fournisseurs. Un aveu sans détour à la barre Interrogé par le président du tribunal, le prévenu a d’emblée reconnu les faits. Il a expliqué avoir souffert un jour d’un mal dont il affirme avoir été guéri après avoir consommé des produits conseillés par un ami. « Le mal est fini », a-t-il déclaré. C’est à la suite de cette expérience qu’il a décidé de se lancer dans la vente de ces produits. Son mode opératoire est simple : il s’approvisionne au marché de Sankaar-Yaar, puis revend sa marchandise sur différents marchés de la capitale, principalement à Hamdallaye, où il exerce habituellement. Selon ses déclarations, sa clientèle est composée de particuliers issus de différentes catégories sociales de Ouagadougou. Paracétamol, sirops, tramadol : une marchandise variée Interrogé sur les produits qu’il commercialise, le prévenu a cité notamment du paracétamol, des sirops, du tramadol et d’autres médicaments. Il a admis savoir que cette activité est interdite, tout en affirmant ignorer les sanctions encourues. Il a également reconnu que cette activité « marche très bien ». 85 000 F CFA retrouvés sur lui lors de son interpellation Le prévenu a été interpellé à Hamdallaye, sur son lieu habituel de vente. Lors de son arrestation, une somme de 85 000 F CFA a été retrouvée sur lui. Il a expliqué que cet argent était destiné à payer un soudeur chargé de réparer sa boutique de téléphonie, qu’il affirme exploiter depuis un certain temps. Il a soutenu que la vente de médicaments ne constituait pas son activité principale. Le silence sur les fournisseurs L’un des points sensibles de l’audience a porté sur l’identité des fournisseurs. Interrogé à deux reprises, Issaka a affirmé ne pas connaître leurs noms. Il a simplement indiqué qu’ils exercent au marché de Sankaar-Yaar et qu’ils sont nombreux à y vendre ces produits. Il a également soutenu ne pas s’approvisionner auprès d’une personne en particulier. Ces réponses n’ont pas convaincu le tribunal, qui a laissé entendre que le prévenu cherchait à protéger ses fournisseurs. Interrogé sur son intention de reprendre cette activité à sa sortie de prison, il a répondu par la négative. Le parquet requiert 24 mois de prison ferme et 10 millions de F CFA d’amende Dans ses réquisitions, le ministère public a rappelé que le prévenu avait reconnu les faits, tout en refusant de désigner ses fournisseurs. Pour le parquet, cette attitude traduit une volonté de ne pas révéler l’identité des personnes auprès desquelles il se ravitaille. Le représentant du ministère public a également estimé que le prévenu pourrait reprendre cette activité après sa libération, d’autant qu’il a lui-même reconnu sa rentabilité. Selon le parquet, cet élément rend peu probable un abandon définitif de ce commerce. Au regard de ces éléments, le ministère public a requis que le prévenu soit déclaré coupable et condamné à 24 mois d’emprisonnement ferme ainsi qu’à une amende ferme de 10 000 000 F CFA. Le tribunal a mis l’affaire en délibéré. Le jugement est attendu le 12 octobre 2026. O. items.title: « Le Rôti » d’Amanda Sthers débarque à Casablanca
items.description: Un simple dîner entre amis peut-il faire voler en éclats toutes les certitudes ? C’est le pari d’Amanda Sthers avec « Le Rôti », une comédie mordante présentée le 15 octobre au Studio des Arts Vivants de Casablanca. Dans le cadre de la programmation des Théâtrales, Top Event Production accueille à Casablanca la nouvelle comédie d’Amanda Sthers, « Le Rôti », mise en scène par Benjamin Elharrar. La pièce sera présentée le jeudi 15 octobre à 20h30 au Studio des Arts Vivants, avec Samy Berry, Vanessa Fery, Valentin Giard et Audrey David au casting. Sur scène, un dîner entre amis va rapidement prendre une tournure inattendue. Jérôme et Mélanie, un couple de Parisiens, reçoivent chez eux Julie, une célibataire pétillante adepte des aventures sans lendemain, ainsi que Mehdi, un collègue de bureau discret et charmant. Tout semble réuni pour passer une agréable soirée. Mais lorsque Mehdi refuse de manger le rôti de porc servi à table pour des raisons religieuses, l’ambiance change progressivement. Une simple remarque en entraîne une autre. Les maladresses s’enchaînent, les non-dits remontent à la surface et les conversations prennent une tournure de plus en plus imprévisible. Derrière les bonnes intentions affichées par chacun, les préjugés et les contradictions finissent par apparaître. Avec « Le Rôti », Amanda Sthers s’empare ainsi de situations du quotidien pour explorer, sur le ton de la comédie, des sujets tels que la religion, les préjugés, l’amitié, le couple ou encore la bonne conscience. Le ressort comique repose notamment sur le décalage entre l’image que les personnages ont d’eux-mêmes et ce qu’ils révèlent lorsque les échanges leur échappent. Au fil des quiproquos et des vérités lancées parfois sans filtre, le dîner devient progressivement le théâtre des contradictions de chacun. Présentée depuis décembre 2025 à la Comédie Saint-Martin à Paris, où elle est programmée jusqu’en mai 2027, « Le Rôti » poursuit son parcours avec cette représentation à Casablanca. The post « Le Rôti » d’Amanda Sthers débarque à Casablanca appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Empire Castel en Afrique : La BRAKINA surpasse les géants du continent en rentabilité avec 63,6 milliards de FCFA de bénéfice net en 2025
items.description: Selon les données publiées par le média spécialisé Horonyafinance.com et issues des comptes sociaux de Brasseries et Glacières Internationales (BGI), les dix principales filiales du groupe Castel en Afrique ont réalisé en 2025 un chiffre d'affaires cumulé de 2,51 milliards d'euros, soit 1 646,46 milliards de FCFA. L'analyse de ces chiffres financiers met en lumière un contraste saisissant : si la filiale camerounaise domine largement en volume de ventes, c'est la filiale burkinabè, la BRAKINA, qui s'impose comme la pépite la plus rentable du portefeuille avec un bénéfice net record de 63,6 milliards de FCFA. L'exercice 2025 s'est inscrit dans une dynamique de croissance marquée pour Castel Afrique, dont le bilan d'activité global fait état d'un chiffre d'affaires dépassant les 3 400 milliards de FCFA, en hausse de 10,3 %. Comme le souligne la synthèse financière relayée par le site Horonyafinance.com, le groupe attribue cette progression à la forte pénétration de ses réseaux de distribution dans 22 pays africains, au réajustement tarifaire et à l'accélération de ses investissements industriels. Au cours de l'année, les usines d’embouteillage ont écoulé 77,1 millions d'hectolitres de boissons, s'appuyant sur un portefeuille de plus de 140 marques parmi lesquelles 33 Export , Beaufort Lager et Castel Beer . Cette performance du pôle boissons a permis d'éponger le recul des activités agricoles de SOMDIA, dont le chiffre d'affaires a fléchi à 516,8 millions d'euros (339 milliards de FCFA). Au total, les dix entités présentées dans les comptes sociaux de BGI totalisent 2,51 milliards d'euros de chiffre d'affaires pour un bénéfice net global de 425 millions d'euros (278,8 milliards de FCFA). Au chapitre des volumes de ventes, les informations diffusées par Horonyafinance.com à partir des rapports de BGI établissent une hiérarchie claire. La Société anonyme des brasseries du Cameroun (SABC) domine nettement le classement des ventes avec un chiffre d'affaires de 736,7 millions d'euros (483,25 milliards de FCFA), concentrant à elle seule près de 30 % du chiffre d'affaires cumulé du groupe. En seconde position, la SOLIBRA en Côte d'Ivoire enregistre 428,4 millions d'euros de ventes (281,01 milliards de FCFA), suivie de près par la Société de fabrication des boissons de Tunisie (SFBT) avec 428,3 millions d'euros. La SOBRAGA au Gabon s’empare de la quatrième place avec 294,4 millions d'euros. La BRAKINA du Burkina Faso pointe quant à elle au cinquième rang avec 243,5 millions d'euros (159,73 milliards de FCFA), représentant environ 10 % des ventes cumulées, devant la SOBEBRA au Bénin et ses 151,6 millions d'euros. C'est sur le terrain du résultat net que le rapport comptable révélé par la presse financière crée la surprise. La BRAKINA s’empare de la première place absolue du portefeuille avec un bénéfice net de 96,9 millions d'euros, soit environ 63,6 milliards de FCFA. À elle seule, la filiale basée au Burkina Faso génère près de 23 % des profits nets cumulés des dix entités BGI. Elle devance la filiale tunisienne SFBT, deuxième en rentabilité avec 88,9 millions d'euros de bénéfice. Le leader commercial, la SABC du Cameroun, doit se contenter de la troisième place du podium des profits avec 77,1 millions d'euros (50,6 milliards de FCFA). Suivent la SOLIBRA (69,8 millions d'euros), la SOBRAGA (56,9 millions d'euros) et la SOBEBRA (38,5 millions d'euros). L'analyse publiée par Horonyafinance.com met également en évidence des performances plus mitigées au sein du groupe. Guinness Cameroun termine l'exercice dans le rouge avec une perte nette de 1,9 million d'euros (1,25 milliard de FCFA), malgré un chiffre d'affaires de 138,2 millions d'euros. La SOBOA au Sénégal affiche également un résultat déficitaire avec une perte de 2,3 millions d'euros (1,51 milliard de FCFA). À l'opposé, la MOCAF en République centrafricaine dégage un bénéfice net de 1,1 million d'euros (721,6 millions de FCFA), tandis que BRAMALI au Mali atteint l'équilibre financier avec un léger gain de 27 000 euros. items.title: Éducation : Le congo supprime le CEPE et prévoit le passage direct de CM2 en 6e dès Juin 2027
items.description: À l'occasion du lancement officiel de la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 au complexe scolaire de Moukoudzi-Ngouaka à Brazzaville, le ministre de l’Enseignement préscolaire, primaire, secondaire et de l’alphabétisation, M. Jean Luc Mouthou, a confirmé la suppression définitive du Certificat d’études primaires élémentaires (CEPE) parmi les examens d’État. Dès le mois de juin 2027, les élèves du CM2 intégreront la classe de 6e grâce à un nouveau format reposant sur le contrôle continu, marquant ainsi une réorganisation en profondeur du système éducatif congolais. Une page se tourne pour l'enseignement primaire en République du Congo. À compter de l'année scolaire 2026-2027, le Certificat d’études primaires élémentaires (CEPE) ne sera plus organisé sous la forme d'un examen national unique. Lors de sa déclaration faite le 1er octobre dernier à Brazzaville, le ministre de l’Enseignement préscolaire, primaire, secondaire et de l’alphabétisation, M. Jean Luc Mouthou, a officialisé la mise en œuvre d'un nouveau format de transition vers le secondaire. En lieu et place de l'épreuve nationale traditionnelle, un Certificat d’études primaires (CEP) sera désormais délivré sur la base du contrôle continu. Dès le mois de juin 2027, ce dispositif permettra un passage direct des élèves de la classe de CM2 vers la classe de 6e, sans passer par un examen d'État. Au-delà de la suppression de l'examen du CEPE, la réforme engagée par le gouvernement réorganise l'architecture même de la scolarité primaire. Le cycle primaire connaîtra une réduction de sa durée globale, passant de six à cinq ans d'études. Cette restructuration repose notamment sur la fusion des classes de CP1 et CP2 en un bloc pédagogique réaménagé. Par cette mesure, l'exécutif entend moderniser l'enseignement primaire et fluidifier le parcours des apprenants vers le premier cycle du secondaire. Ces annonces d'envergure ont été formulées en marge du coup d'envoi officiel de la reprise des cours pour l’année scolaire 2026-2027, donné au complexe scolaire de Moukoudzi-Ngouaka sur l'ensemble du territoire national. Faisant le constat d'une rentrée effective du préscolaire jusqu'au lycée au sein de cet établissement, le ministre s'est réjoui de la reprise des cours. Toutefois, M. Jean-Luc Mouthou a fermement interpellé les parents dont les enfants n'ont pas encore rejoint les bancs de l'école, les exhortant à prendre toutes les dispositions nécessaires pour que chaque élève réintègre sans délai les salles de classe. ? items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: False Flags and Credibility
items.description: Illustration by Abro Last week, reports emerged that an Israeli plumber had thwarted an alleged attempt by the co-pilot of a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv to hijack/crash the aircraft. Interestingly, as further details were made public, social media platforms were flooded with thousands of posts alleging that the incident was a false flag operation orchestrated by the far-right Israeli government and its allied countries’ intelligence agencies. I will not delve into the numerous anomalies highlighted by sceptics, including those raised by active pilots and aviation experts. Instead, this piece focuses on how false flag tactics have begun to backfire. Over the years, significant evidence has emerged demonstrating that staged pretexts have increasingly transitioned from clandestine exceptions to routine instruments of statecraft. Countries using such tactics rely on certain psychological mechanisms that help set up false flag operations. For example, long before a staged provocation takes place, its success is often guaranteed by the cultural and news narratives that precede it. In many countries, movies, television shows and news broadcasts have conditioned audiences to view specific societies through a narrow, negative lens. By repeatedly depicting these populations through recurring tropes of hostility or violence, mainstream media embeds particular perceptions in the public consciousness. Governments have often used media conditioning and false flag operations to make the public more amenable to their agendas. In an age of information warfare, however, scepticism about official narratives is increasing. And scepticism can be a double-edged sword… In their work Manufacturing Consent, media scholars Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky conceptualised this process through their “propaganda model”, demonstrating how mass media functions as an ideological filter, designed to align public perception with official state policy objectives. Rather than presenting objective facts, modern entertainment and news ecosystems construct artificial frames that prompt ordinary citizens to support aggressive foreign policy agendas. When cultural caricatures of ‘enemy’ societies are continuously reinforced, they generate the precise environment required for staged pretexts and/or false flag operations. If a government or intelligence apparatus seeks to fabricate a pretext for military action, global observers rarely question the official narrative, because the alleged culprit matches the villain archetype they have been conditioned to accept by the media. Back in 1922, the American journalist and author Walter Lippmann observed that people construct their worldviews based on simplified “pictures in their heads” created by media narratives, rendering ‘enemy’ populations vulnerable to instant condemnation whenever a security crisis is reported. This dynamic is illustrated across several geopolitical events. During the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Western news outlets and Hollywood routinely depicted Middle Eastern figures through tropes of inherent fanaticism and anti-Western hostility, a phenomenon critically analysed by Edward Said in Orientalism, which showed how cultural production systematically portrays non-Western societies as dangerous. When US and British leaders falsely asserted that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction (WMD), large segments of the public accepted the premise without demanding any serious empirical evidence. The claim naturally aligned with a pre-existing media script. The American media historian Nancy Snow wrote that, across the Cold War, American entertainment and news outlets constantly framed the Soviet Union as a dark, deceitful empire, capable of any atrocity. This persistent framing meant that US covert intelligence operations and exaggerated threats of Soviet terror were accepted almost instantly by a public already conditioned to expect malevolent behaviour from the Soviet regime. However, sometimes, when this tactic is overtly used, the user country can get trapped in its own strategy. For example, the enemy country’s culture may indeed be successfully demonised by propaganda but, eventually, the user country can also start to become widely perceived as a constant engineer of false flag operations. As British media scholar Andrew Hoskins highlights in his research on digital media and conflict, modern hyper-connectivity has fundamentally transformed how the public consumes news during a security crisis. In an era where audiences are routinely exposed to sensationalised reporting, institutional trust has begun to break down. Instead of taking official explanations at face value, global audiences now immediately scrutinise government narratives, moving towards scepticism. This scepticism serves as a vital psychological defence mechanism in an era dominated by ‘information warfare.’ American political scientist Lance Bennett argues that a questioning public is critical for holding power accountable when state actors and media institutions leverage a crisis to manufacture political consent. Questioning official narratives allows citizens to filter out manufactured outrage and demand empirical proof. Indeed, but scepticism can also become a knee-jerk and intellectually lazy exhibition of cynical reflexivity. According to American legal scholar Cass Sunstein, reflexivity that rejects all official accounts can lead to paranoia, where real crises are dismissed as elaborate fabrications. When every high-profile event is instantly dismissed as fake, one crosses into cynicism. Media scholar Renee Hobbs warns that this form of cynicism creates a new cognitive trap. Rather than demanding evidence, individuals simply invert the official narrative to fit their own pre-existing biases. In doing so, the public risks becoming just as easily manipulated by online counter-narratives as they are by official state propaganda. What is truly needed is scepticism that is grounded in deliberate critical thinking. And the good news is that, even amid fierce information wars and state propaganda designed to set the stage for false flag events and despite the knee-jerk reactions that inevitably follow, informed scepticism remains alive. During the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident in the Vietnam War, initial claims by the US government of unprovoked North Vietnamese attacks on American warships were challenged by journalists and naval analysts. Declassified documents later confirmed the attacks were largely fabricated, proving that the US had used them as a pretext for escalating the Vietnam War. Prior to the 1990 Gulf War, testimony claimed Iraqi soldiers were removing Kuwaiti babies from hospital incubators. Sceptical journalists investigated the story and exposed it as a manufactured campaign by the PR firm Hill & Knowlton. In the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, UN weapons inspectors Hans Blix and Scott Ritter, along with reporter Seymour Hersh, challenged intelligence claims about yellowcake uranium and mobile bio-labs in Saddam Hussain’s Iraq. Their demand for physical, forensic proof exposed the flawed WMD narrative woven by the US and UK governments. The manner in which a country’s narrative machinery demonises an adversary to set the stage for false flags has become too predictable a tactic to ignore. Recently, Israel and India have landed in this situation. The frequent reliance on demonising narratives, paired with a global public that increasingly demands empirical proof, has repeatedly forced both countries to present ‘evidence’ that many independent observers find deeply unconvincing. When official explanations fall short under critical scrutiny, it fuels scepticism and solidifies the belief that state propaganda is being actively deployed to justify not-very-pleasant strategic objectives. Published in Dawn, EOS, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Gilgit-Baltistan steps up security for foreigners
items.description: GILGIT: Gilgit-Baltistan police on Saturday decided to strengthen security for Chinese nationals living and working in the region following a high-level meeting to review protective measures for foreigners involved in development projects and business activities. The meeting, chaired by Inspector General of Police (IGP) Dr Akbar Nasir Khan, was held at the Central Police Office in Gilgit, according to a statement issued by the GB police spokesperson. The meeting conducted a review of security arrangements for foreign nationals, particularly Chinese citizens, and assessed measures for those involved in non-CPEC projects, private mining ventures, business activities and those residing at various locations across the region. Senior police officials, including DIG Headquarters, DIG Gilgit Range, AIGs of Special Branch, Operations and Development, SSP SPU and SDPOs from Gilgit district, attended the meeting. The officials reviewed SPU deployments, security directives, and protective measures at check posts and key entry points, while emphasising stronger coordination, advance notification, verification, and security checks for the movement of Chinese nationals across Gilgit, Skardu, Diamer, and other areas. The IGP ordered a fresh district-level threat assessment, identification of security requirements and removal of any shortcomings within a specified timeframe. He also directed implementation of security procedures issued by the National Counter Terrorism Authority, re-verification of residential no-objection certificates (NOC), security audits of approved locations and maintenance of comprehensive records at district level. He called for ensuring compliance with NOC conditions, legal requirements including driving licences, and monitoring of movements, especially during nighttime. He warned that negligence in ensuring the safety of foreign nationals, particularly Chinese citizens, would not be tolerated. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Accès à l’eau potable à Bobo-Dioulasso : Le Ministre Ismaël SOMBIÉ lance un projet majeur pour 132 000 habitants
items.description: Le Ministre d'État, Ministre de l'Agriculture, de l'Eau, des Ressources animales et halieutiques, le Commandant Ismaël SOMBIÉ, a procédé le samedi 10 octobre 2026 au lancement officiel des travaux d'extension du réseau d'eau potable à Bobo-Dioulasso. Destinée à soulager les populations des secteurs 17, 18, 26 et 27, cette initiative vise à alimenter près de 132 000 personnes supplémentaires grâce à la construction d'infrastructures de stockage et de pompage dans un délai de dix mois. Dans la région du Guiriko, la problématique de la desserte en eau potable trouve une réponse concrète avec le lancement d'un important chantier d'infrastructures hydrauliques. À Bobo-Dioulasso, la demande en eau des ménages résidant dans les secteurs 17, 18, 26 et 27 dépassait jusqu'alors la capacité opérationnelle du réseau existant. S'inscrivant dans la vision du Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, le Ministre d'État Ismaël SOMBIÉ a rappelé lors de la cérémonie que l'accès à l'eau potable constitue un droit fondamental et un impératif de dignité et de justice sociale. Le volet technique du projet comprend la réalisation d'une station de pompage d'un débit de 300 m³ par heure, la construction d'un château d'eau d'une capacité de 2 000 m³ et la pose de près de 7 000 mètres linéaires de conduites. Cet ensemble d'ouvrages permettra d'accroître significativement les capacités de pompage, de stockage et de distribution afin d'assurer un approvisionnement régulier en eau potable pour 132 000 personnes supplémentaires. Le calendrier des travaux prévoit une durée d'exécution fixée à dix mois. Pour garantir la réussite de l'opération, le Ministre d'État a adressé une instruction ferme à l'entreprise chargée des travaux concernant le respect strict des délais contractuels et de la qualité des infrastructures. Les équipes techniques et les responsables du suivi ont également été invités à maintenir une présence rigoureuse sur le terrain. Outre Bobo-Dioulasso, cette dynamique d'investissements hydrauliques concerne d'autres grandes agglomérations du pays, notamment Ouahigouya, Koudougou, Fada N'Gourma et Dédougou. items.title: JI links meeting with PM to petroleum levy cut pledge
items.description: LAHORE: Jamaat-i-Islami chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Saturday ruled out meeting Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif without a commitment to abolish the petroleum levy, warning that the party would announce a date for its Islamabad march after Oct 12 if the government failed to provide relief. Addressing a press conference at Mansoorah, the JI chief said statements by ministers suggested that the levy would not be abolished. “If the petroleum levy is not abolished, we have no desire to meet the prime minister,” he said. The premier had sought a meeting with the JI chief after asking the party to suspend its protest march against the levy till then. While Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal conveyed the PM’s message to JI vice chief Liaqat Baloch earlier this week to arrange the meeting, Mr Rehman said talks would serve no purpose without an assurance about the acceptance of JI’s demand. The JI chief demanded meaningful relief for consumers and urged the government to take steps to reap benefit from Saudi Arabia’s reported $5-per-barrel reduction in oil prices for Asian countries. Party threatens to call for Islamabad march if relief is not provided by tomorrow He said the party had staged sit-ins for 42 days against the levy and was continuing its nationwide public meetings and signature campaign. A public meeting is scheduled in Okara today (Sunday). Rejecting the government’s argument that it was constrained by the IMF, Mr Rehman questioned whether similar constraints applied to official spending on luxuries such as an aircraft worth Rs11 billion. On Punjab, Mr Rehman blamed “four decades of family rule” for problems in education and agriculture. He claimed 11,000 schools had been sold and another 25,000 were reportedly listed for sale. He also cited rising agricultural costs, saying the price of a 50kg bag of DAP fertiliser had gone up by Rs3,000. Farmers had received Rs3,000 per maund for wheat, while flour prices had exceeded Rs6,000 per maund and wheat prices had crossed Rs5,000 per maund, he added. Citing poverty estimates, he said the World Bank had put Pakistan’s poverty rate at 23 per cent, while the rate exceeded 40pc under the country’s own criteria. He said Punjab had recorded the largest increase in poverty over the past five years. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Global growth set to slow
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Global economic growth is projected to slow to 2.6 per cent in 2026 and 2.7pc in 2027, from 2.9pc in 2025, while growth in developing economies is expected to fall to 4pc from 4.7pc, amid mounting technological and policy barriers, according to the Trade and Development Report 2026. The flagship report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) finds that governments increasingly use industrial, trade, financial, and technology policies to pursue economic and national security objectives. Access to markets and the ability to move into higher-value activities now depend more heavily on technology, finance and geopolitics. Developing countries will be affected unevenly by the reconfiguration of global trade. Some may emerge as alternative suppliers or intermediary hubs, but sustaining these gains will require stronger productive, regulatory and institutional capabilities, the report warns. Global trade reached a record $35 trillion in 2025. Higher trade values in 2026 are being driven by rising prices amid the energy shock. Trade patterns are also shifting, with trade between China and the United States falling by more than 20pc since 2024, while East Asia has expanded trade with both China and North America. Export controls, investment screening and supply-chain conditions are making it harder for new entrants to access strategic sectors. Asia remains the most dynamic exporting region, with intra-Asian merchandise trade rising markedly. South-South trade is also deepening as China and other major Asian exporters increase shipments to emerging markets. On the import side, Asia is expected to record the strongest growth in 2026, followed by North America, where demand for artificial intelligence-related goods has supported overall imports. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Vente publique de 100 tonnes de riz saisies par la BMCRF : Voici les prix
items.description: La Brigade Mobile de Contrôle économique et de la Répression des Fraudes (BMCRF) organise, le lundi 12 octobre 2026 à partir de 8h00, une importante opération de vente publique portant sur 100 tonnes de riz confisquées pour stockage clandestin. Ouverte aux personnes inscrites comme non encore inscrites, cette vente s'effectuera sur la base de prix officiels homologués par le Ministère de l'Industrie, du Commerce et de l'Artisanat. Dans le cadre des actions de contrôle du marché et de répression des infractions économiques, la Brigade Mobile de Contrôle économique et de la Répression des Fraudes (BMCRF) passe à la phase de liquidation des stocks saisis. Un volume total de 100 tonnes de riz , préalablement confisquées en raison de pratiques de stockage clandestin, sera officiellement remis à la disposition des consommateurs. L'opération de vente est fixée au lundi 12 octobre 2026 à partir de 8h00 , dans les locaux de la BMCRF. Afin d'assurer une participation large, les organisateurs précisent que les personnes déjà inscrites tout comme celles qui ne le sont pas encore sont invitées à se présenter. Pour garantir la transparence des transactions et contrer toute dérive spéculative, les prix de vente ont été formellement arrêtés par le Secrétaire Général du Ministère de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat. Le tableau récapitulatif fixe des tarifs distincts selon les variétés, la brisure et les conditionnements : Riz local (25% brisure, 100% brisure et long grain) : commercialisé au prix unitaire de 10 000 FCFA pour le sac de 25 kg et de 20 000 FCFA pour le sac de 50 kg ; Riz importé 25% brisure étuvé : cédé à 10 000 FCFA le sac de 25 kg et 20 000 FCFA le sac de 50 kg ; Riz importé 100% brisure : affiché à 11 000 FCFA le sac de 25 kg et 22 000 FCFA le sac de 50 kg ; Riz importé 100% brisure (conditionné en sachets de 5 kg) : proposé au tarif de 12 000 FCFA ; Riz importé 25% brisure riz blanc : fixé à 10 000 FCFA le sac de 25 kg et 20 000 FCFA le sac de 50 kg. En remettant sur le marché ces 100 tonnes de riz saisies sous le contrôle direct de l'administration, l'opération vise à réapprovisionner le circuit de distribution à des prix régulés. Le public concerné est attendu le lundi 12 octobre à partir de 8h00 au sein de la BMCRF. items.title: Tension over fresh crude oil discovery in Delta community
items.description: •Family kicks against purported land lease to firm By Godwin Oritse Crude oil discovery has sparked a dispute in Okpe-Isoko community, Delta State, with the Adhakpor family rejecting a purported land lease agreement allegedly entered into with Sterling Global Limited for the exploration and development of the oil-bearing property. The Adhakpor family rejected a purported lease agreement allegedly executed by individuals claiming to represent it, saying they had no authority or mandate to act on its behalf. In a statement, the family said it neither authorised nor mandated any individual or group to negotiate, execute or enter into any lease agreement, Memorandum of Understanding, MOU, or any related document with Sterling Global Limited concerning its land. Describing the purported transaction as unauthorised and unacceptable, the family stressed that no individual could validly bind it to any agreement without a specific mandate duly granted by it. It further stated that its duly constituted and elected executives, together with other authorised representatives, had been formally empowered to represent the family’s interests and handle negotiations, engagements and documentation relating to its land. The family, therefore, disassociated itself from any agreement, commitment or undertaking purportedly entered into by persons acting without its express authorisation, warning that such actions should not be construed as representing its position or interests. According to the family, the authorised representatives emerged from a resolution reached at its general meeting held on October 4, 2026. It consequently directed that all negotiations, documentation, execution and implementation of any lease or other transaction involving the Adhakpor family’s land must henceforth be conducted exclusively through the duly authorised representatives presented by the family. The family also made it clear that it does not recognise or accept any purported lease, MOU or related document entered into by persons who were not duly authorised to represent it. It warned all parties, prospective investors and other stakeholders dealing with the family’s land to ensure that they engage only with the duly recognised representatives, saying any transaction undertaken outside the authority granted by the family would be without its mandate and should not be construed as binding on the Adhakpor family. “This position is intended to ensure transparency, accountability, proper representation, unity, peace, and the protection of the rights and interests of the Adhakpor family.” The statement stated. Meanwhile, the Adhakpor family alleged that a community leader, in collaboration with some members of the community, unlawfully introduced persons who are not members of the family into the negotiation committee. The family strongly objected to the development, saying that only duly recognised members of the Adhakpor family should be involved in any committee constituted to negotiate or deliberate on matters concerning the family’s interests. Reacting to the development, the Head of the Adhakpor family, Chief Ide Abade, told Sunday Vanguard that he was arrested by the community leadership over his opposition to the purported lease agreement with Sterling Global Limited. He added that the family had concluded plans to seek redress through the courts as non-members of the family had no authority to negotiate or enter into any agreement concerning the family’s land. Similarly, the President of the Okpe-Isoko Community, Chief Fred Efeh, told Sunday Vanguard that the Adhakpor family was duly represented on the committee constituted to negotiate the lease agreement. Efeh said the controversy arose from a disagreement between two branches, or “gates,” of the Adhakpor family over ownership of the land where an oil well was discovered. His words: “The Adhakpor family they are talking about has two gates. It is one of the gates that has come to complain.” He explained that one branch claimed its forefather had shared the land and that the portion where the oil was discovered belonged exclusively to it. “One of the gates said their father had shared that land. And the portion where the oil is, is solely their own”. Efeh, however, said the other branch maintained that proceeds from the land, including palm trees and other natural resources, should benefit the entire Adhakpor family. “The other one is saying, no, that the palm trees and all other natural resources that may come from there are supposed to be for all of them, not only one gate of the Adhakpor family”. He said following the discovery of the oil well, the company involved in the exploration approached the traditional institution and the community, in line with established procedures. “So when the oil exploration came, the company duly, as ought to be done, came to the palace and came to the community. I, as the president general, was present”, he added. According to him, after the necessary consultations, a negotiation committee comprising representatives of the two branches of the Adhakpor family was constituted. “After fulfilling all normal ways of entering the land, we started negotiation. So the family, these two gates, we now formed a committee for negotiation, where the Adhakpor family people were truly represented,” he said. Efeh, however, said some representatives later withdrew from the negotiation, leading to the current dispute. “As we were going along on the negotiation, they withdrew,” he said, adding that the disagreement centred on the composition of the committee. His position contrasts with that of the Adhakpor family, which has rejected the purported lease agreement and maintained that the persons involved lacked the mandate to represent the family or enter into any agreement concerning its land. Efforts to obtain the reaction of the Community Relations Manager, Sterling Oil Exploration and Energy Production Company (SEEPCO), Mr. Rotimi Bakari, were unsuccessful. Bakari told Sunday Vanguard that he could not respond to the queries over the telephone and requested that the correspondent visit his office in Warri, Delta State, for further discussion. Efforts to obtain the reaction of the traditional ruler of the community, the Ovie of Okpe-Isoko, proved unsuccessful as calls and messages sent to his telephone lines were neither answered nor responded to as of press time. Delta Schools: Beyond the prism of cynics By Kennedy Mbele Against the backdrop of recent negative reports in a section of the media, majority of public primary and secondary schools across Delta State are in good shape and conducive for effective teaching and learning. The fallacious judgment of using the state of Otor-Edo Primary School in Ughelli South Local Government Area to reach a sweeping generalized judgment of “poor state of public schools” in the state is quite unfortunate and thoroughly misleading Yes, there is no denying that some public schools require urgent intervention. Old classroom blocks, inadequate furniture, damaged facilities, and vandalism remain realities in some communities This ( intervention) is only a natural and logical way to sustain wholesome development in any given society, and both individuals, corporate organizations and the government, quite widely, follow this path. But a closer look at schools in Ughelli South Local Government Area reveals that, across the board, the vast majority are not decrepit as the authors of the fallacious work would want to paint. Besides, the state government, under Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, has put his potent hands to the plough, and is doing a lot to improve on school infrastructure in the state. For instance, a visit to Okutu Primary School, Otokutu; Makpa Primary School, Oginibo; and Baba-Ido Primary School, Okwagbe, provides an instructive picture At Okutu Primary School, the Headteacher, Mrs Joy Ebireri, commended Governor Oborevwori for his interventions, pointing to a newly constructed three-classroom block and pupils’ desks provided by the government. She said the intervention has brought considerable relief to the school, saying; “we are happy with the intervention. The new classrooms have made a positive difference, and you can see how happy the children are to use them”. The new classrooms, according to Ebireri, have elicited so much enthusiasm that it has been assigned to pupils to provide a more conducive environment for learning. She, however, decried the spate of vandalism, which, according to her, had compounded the infrastructure problem. Ebireri said, for instance, that her office had been vandalised, thus forcing her to operate from a classroom. “My present office is not supposed to be an office. It is actually a classroom. We had to move here temporarily because my former office was vandalised. The roof was removed and the building could no longer accommodate us,” she lamented The experience at Makpa Primary School, Oginibo, is slightly different but equally revealing. Assistant Headteacher, Mrs Rita Akata, commended the State Government for constructing a new classroom block after the devastating impact of the 2022 flood which, she said, damaged facilities and disrupted learning. She said; “we are grateful to the government for coming to our aid. The flood destroyed part of the school, but the new building has helped to improve the learning environment for the pupils,” Akata said This pattern of a new lease of life is the same across most public schools in the state. Meanwhile, Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, while commissioning the Model Technical College, Oghareki in Ethiope West Local Government Area, on Friday, directed for the complete overhaul of all dilapidated public primary and secondary schools across the state. The implementation of this directive is expected to further consolidate the quality and quantity of infrastructure available in public basic and secondary schools But even before the directive is effected, it is instructive to note that Oborevwori’s directive is a display of a government that is genuinely committed to providing conducive teaching and learning environment for teachers, pupils and students. items.title: Sécurité au Burkina Faso et en Côte d’Ivoire : La Police nationale burkinabè met hors d’état de nuire un redoutable gang armé ciblant les points de transfert et acheteurs d’or
items.description: Grâce à une opération conjointe menée par plusieurs services spécialisés de la Police Nationale et à la collaboration précieuse des populations, quatorze membres actifs d'un dangereux réseau de braqueurs armés ont été interpellés dans la région du Djôrô. Principalement composé de repris de justice, ce gang transfrontalier hyper-structuré écumait les commerces, boutiques de transfert d'argent et sites d'orpaillage à travers le Burkina Faso et la Côte d'Ivoire. C'est la fin d'un long cauchemar pour les commerçants et les acteurs économiques de plusieurs régions du Burkina Faso et des pays voisins. Le Service Régional de la Police Judiciaire (SRPJ) du Djôrô, appuyé par la Division des Investigations Criminelles (DIC), le Commissariat Central de Police de Bogandé et la Direction du Matériel et du Budget de la Police Nationale, a réussi à démanteler une bande armée particulièrement active. Le réseau, constitué en majorité de repris de justice, ne limitait pas ses exactions au seul territoire national. Leurs tentacules s'étendaient de Ouagadougou à Gaoua, en passant par Pouytenga, Houndé, Dano ou Diébougou, jusqu'aux villes ivoiriennes de Doropo et Bouaké. Rien n'était laissé au hasard par cette organisation criminelle où chaque membre occupait un rôle strictly défini. Le groupe ciblait en priorité les établissements détenant d'importantes liquidités, notamment les boutiques Orange Money, les stations-services, les fonderies ainsi que les acheteurs d'or. Après un repérage minutieux et une réunion de planification, les malfrats opéraient par binômes à moto, le visage dissimulé sous des cache-nez, des casquettes et des pullovers. Sur le théâtre des opérations, la répartition des tâches était militaire : pendant que des complices armés de fusils assuraient le guet et tiraient des coups de sommation pour tenir les riverains à distance, d'autres dépouillaient les victimes sous la menace d'armes blanches. En cas de moindre résistance, les braqueurs n'hésitaient pas à faire usage de leurs armes pour abattre froidement leurs cibles. Le fonctionnement financier de la bande répondait à des règles précises : une partie du butin prélevé servait à payer la location des armes, le reste étant distribué au prorata de l'implication de chacun. Privilégiant l'argent liquide, les braqueurs abandonnaient systématiquement les téléphones portables volés pour échapper au traçage des enquêteurs. La vigilance des forces de l'ordre et l'appui citoyen ont néanmoins permis d'appréhender quatorze (14) membres actifs du réseau. Lors des perquisitions, la police a mis la main sur un impressionnant arsenal comprenant deux fusils à pompe, un fusil de chasse, quatre pistolets automatiques, des chargeurs, des munitions, des armes blanches, ainsi qu'un véhicule, plusieurs motos et des appareils électroménagers. Saluant l'appui déterminant des populations qui a rendu possible ce coup de filet, la Police Nationale a renouvelé ses remerciements envers les citoyens. L'institution invite par ailleurs les commerçants et opérateurs économiques à ne pas garder de fortes sommes d'argent liquide sur leurs lieux de travail et à redoubler de prudence lors des transactions financières. Enfin, les autorités rappellent l'importance de poursuivre la dynamique de dénonciation de tout individu ou comportement suspect via les numéros verts gratuits 17, 16 et 1010. items.title: Israeli strikes kill five in Gaza
items.description: CAIRO: Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Saturday, health officials said. Medics said an Israeli strike killed four people near Panda Mall in Gaza City, whi­le another killed one person in the Tuffah neighbourhood further south of the city. Israel, which claims Hamas has been rea­­rming and launching attacks in violation of an October ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. Hamas has denied trying to carry out att­a­cks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Isr­ael of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Last year’s US-brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Israeli air strikes have continued, with at least 1,400 Palestinians killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while Israel claims four of its soldiers have been killed. Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched in October 2023. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

items.title: Why kidnappers target NYSC members — Security experts
items.description: •About 40 abducted in one year By Nnamdi Ojiego The abduction of 20 prospective members of the National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, in Imo State has brought into sharper focus the growing danger facing young Nigerians travelling to or from orientation camps and places of primary assignment. The 20 graduates, who were travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states, were abducted on October 1 along the Owerri-Onitsha Road in Imo State. They were rescued on October 7, after seven days in captivity, in a joint operation involving the police, military, Department of State Services, DSS, and other security agencies. The victims were subsequently taken for medical examination and treatment. The Imo incident came barely weeks after another mass abduction involving NYSC members in Kogi State. On August 26, 16 corps members returning from the NYSC orientation camp in Bayelsa State to Abuja after completing their orientation were abducted along the Aloma-Egane axis in Ofu Local Government Area of Kogi State. All 16 were later rescued after a coordinated operation involving the Armed Forces, police, DSS and local vigilantes. The two incidents have renewed concerns over the safety of corps members whose national service often requires them to undertake long journeys through unfamiliar parts of the country and, in some cases, known kidnapping corridors. They also form part of a wider pattern recorded over the past year. According to Sunday Vanguard findings, not less than 40 corps members and prospective corps members have been reported abducted in separate incidents, including the January abduction of prospective corps member, Binuyo Lateefah, in Kogi State while travelling to Taraba; the April abduction of prospective corps member, Gift David Samiya, on the Akwanga-Jos road while travelling to Maiduguri; the April abduction of LASU graduate, Ogunlana Adetola Sodiq, while travelling to an orientation camp in Osun State, and the May abduction of serving corps member, Eunice Ameh, in Abuja. Lateefah was reportedly held for 10 days after her abduction on January 22, while her abductors demanded N30 million. Ameh, an Abuja-based lawyer and corps member, was abducted in Maitama on May 6 and released four days later after money was reportedly paid, although the amount was not disclosed. In the Kogi case, one of the rescued corps members, David Ayodele, later recounted that the abductors beat and kicked their captives and threatened to keep them in the forest for a month and kill them. The Imo victims also spent a week in captivity before their rescue. Police said security operatives had earlier located the kidnappers’ camp through drone surveillance but delayed moving in after intelligence indicated that the area had been mined with improvised explosive devices. The Imo State Commissioner of Police, Audu Bosso, has since said he was not aware that ransom was paid for the release of the corps members, saying the kidnappers eventually succumbed to pressure from security forces operating in the forest. Predictability of deployment For security governance expert, Prof. Al Chukwuma Okoli, the vulnerability of corps members is linked to the predictability of their deployment and movement. He said: “The vulnerability arises from predictable posting to high-risk rural areas that are grossly under-policed. Corps members travel on hazardous highways bereft of real-time security. “Posting corps members to volatile areas without contingency plans to secure their movements through convoy tracking and risk-map deployment poses a challenge.” He argued that the Federal Government, NYSC and security agencies should jointly develop a system for protecting corps members from the point of departure to their destination. “Government and NYSC authority need to work closely with security agencies to jointly fund safe transit protocols, secure corps members’ lodges, and ensure that there is a rapid-response mechanism to rescue victims when an attack occurs.” Okoli also linked the difficulty in rescuing victims and bringing kidnappers to justice to the absence of effective state security presence in some of the areas where the attacks occur. “Such kidnappings occur in areas with limited coercive state presence and inadequate security, making rapid rescue response challenging”, he said adding that prosecution had also suffered from “weak inter-agency collaboration in case treatment.” Weakness of intelligence systems For Alfred Ononugbo, a forensic investigator and criminal intelligence specialist, the wider problem is rooted in the weakness of Nigeria’s intelligence and policing systems. According to him, “the crime of kidnapping has lingered due to the absence of credible intelligence, national crime database and ineffective policing.” Ononugbo said the absence of reliable crime data makes it difficult for security agencies to understand patterns of kidnapping across states and communities and deploy appropriate responses. “No reliable data to provide peculiar crime behaviours with states and communities within the country in order to develop necessary security responses to such crime patterns”, he said noting that criminals tend to identify victims who are vulnerable and capable of generating quick ransom payments. “The intending corp members may have been victims of opportunistic attack or informants considering that they may have given away their identities as a uniformed group on transit. The criminals often target the most vulnerable and beneficial victims to generate quick revenues and escape from the consequences of their crimes.” He said stops made during long journeys could also provide opportunities for criminals to gather information about the passengers. “They may have attracted attention at locations where they stop during the trip and this made it possible for the information to be passed to the kidnappers.” He recommended a more deliberate security arrangement for corps members travelling in groups. “Considering the challenge of attacks by criminals, an armed security escorts for the young graduates should have been appropriate for such movement. ” Fundamentally evidence-driven Ononugbo also criticised the country’s capacity to investigate and prosecute kidnapping cases, saying criminal prosecution is fundamentally evidence-driven. “With science and technology, forensic evidences provides accurate evidence harvesting, handling and presentations in courts to help prosecutors and the courts.” But he said the police face serious difficulties in conducting actionable investigations, citing inadequate training, weak exposure to modern intelligence techniques and deficiencies in evidence gathering. “Modern technology and digital solutions must be inculcated in the training of our policemen and women.” He further identified alleged collusion and compromise as another obstacle to fighting kidnapping. “Collusion and compromise is another setback to minimising kidnapping crimes as some of the financial evidence are often tempered with by unprofessional and poorly disciplined personnel”, he alleged. Ononugbo called for improved training, better remuneration and greater use of technology, while urging government to involve traditional institutions and town development associations in community policing. “We must improve on training, capacity building and the use of modern technology in combating kidnapping and other forms of crimes”, he added. National concern For Okechukwu Nwanguma, Executive Director of the Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre, RULAAC, the recurring abduction of corps members should concern the country because national service is compulsory. He pointed out that the obligation placed on young graduates by the NYSC scheme creates a corresponding responsibility for the government to protect them. “The recurring kidnapping of National Youth Service Corps members should concern every Nigerian because these are young citizens undertaking a compulsory national assignment. If the State requires young graduates to travel across the country in the service of national integration, then there is a corresponding duty to take reasonable measures to protect them from foreseeable harm”, Nwanguma stated. Deployment pattern He explained that corps members face the wider security problems affecting Nigerian highways, but their deployment pattern creates additional exposure, stressing that the recent Imo incident demonstrated the problem. “They frequently travel long distances to unfamiliar parts of the country, sometimes using ordinary commercial transport and passing through roads with known histories of kidnapping and armed attacks. “The problem therefore goes beyond advising corps members to ‘be security conscious.’ Government needs a systematic risk assessment of routes used by prospective and serving corps members.” He called on NYSC to work with the police, DSS and other security agencies to identify kidnapping hotspots and establish safer travel arrangements during mobilisation and demobilisation. “Where a route presents a demonstrably high security risk, government should consider coordinated transportation from designated departure points, security-supported movement during peak mobilisation periods, or alternative deployment arrangements.” According to him, graduates should not be forced into a choice between obeying their NYSC call-up instructions and exposing themselves to known security threats. “Young Nigerians should not be compelled to choose between obeying an NYSC call-up instruction and exposing themselves to a foreseeable risk of kidnapping.” Nwanguma also called for a joint security protocol involving the Federal Government, NYSC, state governments and security agencies. Such a protocol, he said, should cover prevention, emergency response, communication with families, rescue operations and post-rescue care. “NYSC should maintain a constantly updated security map of deployment and travel routes and communicate specific warnings to corps members before they travel. “Reporting dates should also take account of travel distances so that prospective corps members are not pressured into unsafe travel schedules.” The RULAAC director said security agencies needed stronger intelligence coverage and patrols along identified kidnapping corridors, while state governments should improve roads and support intelligence gathering in vulnerable communities. The Imo incident, he said, illustrated why prevention and intelligence gathering should receive as much attention as rescue operations. “That underscores why prevention and intelligence must receive as much attention as rescue operations after people have already been abducted.” Nwanguma also warned that the consequences of kidnapping do not end when victims regain their freedom. “There should also be proper psychosocial and medical support for rescued victims. Kidnapping can leave serious psychological consequences even after physical freedom has been regained.” On prosecution, he described accountability as one of the weakest parts of Nigeria’s response to kidnapping. “Public attention understandably concentrates on securing the victims’ release, but there is often much less information afterwards about identifying, arresting and successfully prosecuting the perpetrators”, he said. According to him, the difficulty of operating in forests and remote communities, movement across state boundaries, the use of disposable telephones and the need to prioritise hostages’ lives can complicate investigations. But he also pointed to institutional weaknesses. “Weak intelligence coordination, poor preservation of evidence, difficulties securing witnesses, inadequate forensic capacity and delays in investigation and prosecution can undermine accountability”, he said. According to him, there is an important difference between rescuing a hostage and dismantling a kidnapping network. Hos words: “Recovering a kidnapped person is an immediate humanitarian success, but dismantling the criminal network requires identifying the kidnappers, their informants, financiers, ransom collectors, arms suppliers and other collaborators, and then assembling evidence capable of sustaining prosecution.” He urged the government to publish anonymised data showing kidnapping cases investigated, suspects arrested, prosecutions and convictions. “This would allow Nigerians to assess whether criminal networks are actually being dismantled rather than simply displaced.” For the experts, the answer lies in moving security planning beyond the orientation camps to the roads corps members must use to reach them and return home. As Nwanguma put it, the central issue is the responsibility of the state to protect those it requires to serve. “The objective should not merely be to rescue corps members after they have been abducted. It should be to make their abduction far less likely in the first place and to ensure that those who attack them face credible investigation, prosecution and punishment”, he stated. The post Why kidnappers target NYSC members — Security experts appeared first on Vanguard News .
