items.title: Abuja declaration: S/West leaders, ACF disagree with Igbo
items.description: •.as restructuring agitation resurfaces ahead of polls By Dayo Johnson, Dapo Akinrefon, Olasukanmi Akoni, Dickson Omobola, Rotimi Ojomoye, Deola Badru Barely three months to the 2027 general elections, the controversy generated by the position of the Igbo Leaders of Thought, ILT, on the restructuring of Nigeria, yesterday, provoked mixed reactions from South-West and northern leaders, with some describing aspects of the proposal as unrealistic and capable of causing political destabilisation. The ILT had rejected the communiqué issued at the Abuja restructuring conference of August 20, 2026, accusing the organisers of disregarding the position of the Igbo delegation. The group proposed a 10-region political structure for Nigeria, with regional control of resources and regional police, while calling for the temporary suspension of the 2027 general elections pending the completion of the restructuring exercise. The ILT also proposed an enlarged Igbo Region extending beyond the five South-East states, and called for the restructuring exercise to be completed before May 2027, after which elections would be conducted under a new constitutional arrangement. The proposal has triggered a fresh debate over the structure of the Nigerian federation, the place of regionalism, the future of the existing 36-state arrangement, resource control, regional policing and the implications of delaying the 2027 elections. Reacting to the development in chats with Sunday Vanguard, South-West and northern voices differed on the precise form restructuring should take, but several questioned the ILT’s approach and particularly its proposal to suspend elections. Their position is unrealistic—Adejumo Speaking on the matter, Mogaji Gboyega Adejumo, who led the South-West Zone to the Patriots Constitutional Conference in Abuja, said the position of the Igbo Leaders of Thought was unrealistic, arguing that the various ethnic groups in Nigeria appeared to be struggling to identify the precise solution to the country’s structural problems. Adejumo, who took a swipe at the Igbo Leaders of Thought over some of their positions, said the confusion was not peculiar to the Igbo, but reflected a wider failure among Nigeria’s constituent groups to determine what they wanted from the Nigerian project. He said: “What I can say is this, the Igbo are as confused as any. Most of the tribes in Nigeria are in that kind of situation of confusion, of knowing absolutely what next to do. “It could still be part of the main frustration coming out of the fact that no region, except perhaps the core North, is fully enjoying being in this contraption called Nigeria. “But again, to be critical and to be discretionary is to look at the whole matter of our coming together, unity, existence as a nation. It is faulty right from the beginning, we know.” Going down memory lane, Adejumo said several attempts had been made to resolve Nigeria’s structural problems, but without producing a lasting solution. “Many attempts have been made but nothing so concrete has come out,” he said. “Again, restructuring that has now been in the front burner for many years now is not new. It’s what the Action Group government started to do or had started to do since 1951, culminating in the 1953 London Conference. It is restructuring. “It is because the structure was disrupted in 1962, that is why we now say we want to restructure.” Igbo, Fulani According to him, the South-West proposal presented at the Patriots Constitutional Conference was not fundamentally different from some of the demands being made by the Igbo. He said: “What exactly are the Igbo saying? They said they reject the recent attempt in Abuja. I was the leader of the South-West Zone that went to the Patriots Constitutional Conference in Abuja and we presented the South-West proposal. “Now, it is no different from what the South-West has always advocated for, which is not diametrically different from what the Igbo are saying. “The only thing that is different is that the Igbo seem to not know what exactly is the situation with our problem, where the trouble lies.” Adejumo argued that the fundamental issue was not simply the question of which region got what, but how the constituent parts of Nigeria could negotiate a workable political arrangement. “Between the Igbo and the Fulani, somehow the idea of coming into a union is not about the spread. It’s about what each other can get. It is not about making sure that everybody has got something but trying to corner whatever is left to themselves,” he said. Awolowo, 1966 and 1979 Adejumo also went into the history of the relationship among the major ethnic groups, particularly the political choices made by the Igbo and Yoruba at different periods of Nigeria’s history. He said: “1959 going towards 1960, the Igbo, rather than take the Prime Ministership, they decided to go into partnering with the North. Everybody didn’t bother to, in any way, begin to complain. We just went back to our shell and began to do our thing.” He also referred to the 1966 coup and the subsequent Civil War. “Same thing, well, the Civil War started and it was blamed on the Igbo on January 15, 1966. I’ve done many interviews ever before, but Ibrahim Babangida came out and said it was not an Igbo coup. It was not an Igbo coup.” According to him, the political relationship between the Igbo and the North continued after the Civil War, including in the Second Republic. “But then, with all that the Igbo suffered in 1979, they still went back into an arrangement with the North, leaving the South West,” he said. He recalled a statement attributed to the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo concerning the consequences of the secession of the Eastern Region. “Obafemi Awolowo said something. He said, whether by acts of omission or commission, if the Igbo are allowed to leave, then the Yoruba will not stay. “How is it that people just don’t understand that question? The Igbo determined that to mean that Awolowo promised the Igbo that he would leave. “Was Awolowo a soldier? Did he even have a gun? Was he the military head of the South West as at that time? Was he like an Ojukwu figure? Could he even declare anything beyond his household? “But what Awolowo was saying was simple. Nigeria stands on a tripod. The North, the South, and the East. If you allow the East to go, it will just be the North and the West. And that will be a disaster for the West. “We will never be able to grow. We will never be able to even breathe. So, it is better for the three of us to stand together, rather than for one part, the Igbo, to go and the Yoruba to suffer.” Choices Adejumo said the political choices of the different groups over the years should inform the current restructuring debate rather than be used to deepen ethnic divisions. He said the South-West had consistently pushed for restructuring, recalling the various constitutional conferences and political initiatives that preceded the current debate. According to him, the Yoruba position had evolved through the 1979-78 Constituent Assembly, the 1991 process associated with Alao-Aka Bashorun, the Abacha era and the 2014 National Conference. “Now, that will not happen. So, the Igbo had to stay. But in staying in 1979, what did they do? They teamed up with the North. The Yoruba didn’t complain. “Now, we have a situation where the Awolowo School of Thought, and everything that had always won over the South West, lost out to a new regime led by Bola Tinubu that took the Yoruba, for the very first time, to join with the North. “And all hell is let loose. But who are the people leading the charge that we must balance it? It’s the Yoruba.” Adejumo said the South-West delegation to the Patriots Conference did not depart substantially from the historical Yoruba demand for restructuring. “And when we went to that constitutional conference, of which I was the leader, we presented nothing short of what has been the confluence of all thoughts,” he said. “Right from 1953 to what we went to discuss in the 1979-78, Constituent Assembly, to the 1991 profound statement of Alao-Aka Bashorun, and that was where the idea of restructuring started afresh. 2004, 1999, Abacha and everything that they did, the Yoruba wanted out.” 2014 Confab He also criticised the political handling of the recommendations of the 2014 National Conference. “Now, let us now look at the 2014 CONFAB, which was largely a nefarious affair. But at the same time, we had perhaps the best of all that has happened since the 1963 constitution. “But Nigeria, in their wisdom, chose Buhari, who was never ever going to honour that 2014 CONFAB report, which gave everything to everyone. If you want regionalism, go for it. If you want statism, go for it.” Adejumo said the Yoruba position was not necessarily a return to the old regional arrangement in which all states within a geographical area would automatically be subordinated to one regional authority. “The Yoruba will always want regionalism, but along with statism. Because the Ondo man will say, I’m not going back to Ibadan. The Ekiti man will say, I’m not going back to Ibadan. “But the question I always tell them is, is Abuja nearer to you than Ibadan?” He also questioned the practicality of calls for a Yoruba nation. “Here we are, even within the Yoruba, some people are shouting for Yoruba nation. But where is the pathway? I don’t see it. Where will the boundaries be? Who will you sit down with? Who is the arbitrator? “Who is going to sit down with you and say, okay, this is the boundary between Yoruba land and the North, or the East, or even anywhere else? So, it was all a farce.” ‘What exactly do the Igbo want?’ Turning specifically to the latest position of the Igbo Leaders of Thought, Adejumo questioned what he described as inconsistencies in the group’s demands. “Now, talking about what the Igbo have just put out. Is it any different from what was said at Aburi, that was rejected? You want resource control, you want this, you want that. You reject restructuring. “So, what exactly do you want?” He recalled his involvement with Afenifere and the formation of the Southern and Middle Belt Leaders Forum, SMBLF, saying efforts had been made to create a broad platform for the various southern and Middle Belt groups. “I was a spokesperson for Afenifere. I spent many years in Afenifere. But look at the way we wanted to even bring some kind of solution. “In 2017, we had the Yoruba Agenda spread all over again in the Ibadan Declaration. And we invited, well, the Ndi-Igbo in Ohanaeze, and the PANDEF of the South-South, and the Middle-Belt Forum. Come and see what we are doing. “So, we formed the Southern and Middle Belt Leaders Forum, SMBLF.” He said Afenifere’s independence from government was important to its position. “Afenifere, we are not affiliated to any government, any state government. Because he who pays the piper, dictates the tune. “We were doing our thing, and we could not be moved, we could not be influenced by any government, state, federal, or local.” ‘Where is the mass movement?’ Adejumo also questioned the practical route to the creation of separate nations from Nigeria. “The only way you can create a nation out of any nation is by mass movement,” he said. “If the people rise and say this is it, and they are not relenting, most likely they are going to get it. “Or there is a serious crisis, chaos, in which even the government is not existing anymore. Then you could create something out of something. Or perhaps by consensus, you all sat down and say, okay, now let us break up. “So, where is the mass movement now? Where is the crisis? Where is the chaos? So, why create nothing out of it? Why try to create something out of nothing?” He said the approaching election made it even more difficult to pursue such an agenda. “Everybody is focused on the election. This election, we don’t know what the outcome will be. But, even if there is going to be a recourse to something, it will have to be after the election. “It will have to be after that election.” Adejumo said the various groups should concentrate on achieving workable reforms rather than making demands that lacked a clear pathway to implementation. ‘Go back and think about Igbo liberation’ He advised the Igbo Leaders of Thought to reconsider their approach and build alliances with other groups. “So, in all of this, what is taking over? I don’t think we have conviction anymore in this country. I think what we have are personal interests, not even sectional interests. “So the Leaders of Thought should better go back and think very well about how the Igbo people can be liberated.” He said the Igbo needed to work with other groups rather than pursue a strategy in isolation. “Who is talking about him? It’s largely forgotten. So, what the Igbo need to do is go back to the drawing board and come up with something realistic and begin to liaise with other groups. “We have to understand what we want out of Nigeria.” Adejumo warned that separation itself did not automatically guarantee stability or prosperity. “Everybody is saying we want to go separate ways but if that is so easy and that will guarantee that each path will survive, what are the guarantees? I can see none. “I can only see Sudan that even after separation, there is a continuation of war. I can see Ethiopia and Eritrea but if we want the kind of separation that brought about USSR, fine, let’s walk towards that. That’s dialogue. “If we want to be like United States of America, it is still about dialogue.” He ultimately advocated negotiation among the various constituent groups. “So I would rather we choose a dialogue so that we can at least know that we can settle things amicably. “The Nigerian question is, where are we, all of us? Where are the Yorubas? Where are the Igbo? Where are the Middle-Elders? Where are the South-South? Where is the Core-North? “Are we exactly where we want ourselves to be? If the Yoruba said this is what we want, we want the maximum strength of us Yoruba to go and negotiate. Let the Igbo too come with their own. Do not leave anyone behind.” Regionalism will cause destabilisation — Afenifere Pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, also rejected the proposal for regionalism, warning that it could create fresh political instability, particularly in areas with significant minority populations. National Publicity Secretary of the group, Justice Faloye, said the organisation remained committed to the resolutions of the 2014 National Conference. Faloye said: “Until another wider representative sovereign conference is held, Afenifere stands on the 2014 Confab Resolutions, made up with a wide and balanced delegation, which, after thorough deliberations, agreed on States as Federating Units. “The very reason Afenifere had to step down from regionalism is what transpired in Abuja, where the Igbo delegation accused Yorubas of backing Ijaws and walked out. “Regionalism will cause disaffection, especially in South-South and North Central regions. Regionalism will cause great political destabilization that will arise from allocating states and ethnicities to regions from above. “Nigeria is made up of 371 ethnicities, so how do we allocate them to regions for representative governance?” Faloye said the 2014 Conference had already provided an alternative approach. “At the Confab, it was agreed that states with the same ethnicity that want to amalgamate into one region are free to do so, if voted for amongst themselves. “It was also agreed that ethnicities in local governments are free to vote to join neighbouring states. “This will make the whole process bottoms up whereby people can decide their representation from local governments upwards, and not a top down approach whereby peoples are allocated to arbitrary regions from the Federal Government downwards.” He described imposed regionalism as problematic. “Regionalism is at best internal colonization, and at worst, a diversionary tactic by those that don’t want to do anything but to derail real restructuring.” Afenifere: ‘We stand by 2014 Confab’ The Secretary General of Afenifere, Chief Ademola Folarin, said the organisation was not part of the Abuja conference and had not changed its position on the 2014 Confab. Folarin said: “Afenifere was not part of the Abuja Conference. “The position of Afenifere has not changed from the one established by the 2014 Confab, where duly accredited representatives of Nigerian nationalities, by consensus, passed 600 resolutions. “The resolutions included the retention of federal/state structure, with the possible creation of more states to accommodate minorities. “With the states having the power and right to merge or de-merge through a well established constitutional process. The creation of regions was jettisoned, essentially to protect minorities.” He said the conference had also advocated substantial devolution of powers. “It was also resolved that more powers should be devolved to the STATES, including policing, mining, local government and so on and so forth. The proceedings and resolutions of the 2014 are well documented. “Afenifere stands by them, until the duly accredited representatives of the nationalities meet to vary them.” Restructuring must be by consent— Omololu The Convener, Conscience of Yoruba Nation Group, Apagun Kole Omololu, however, supported restructuring into autonomous regions, but insisted that the process must be based on the consent of the communities concerned. Omololu said the South-West position was clear in supporting autonomous regions within a voluntary, inclusive and cooperative federal system. He said: “The South-West position is clear: we support the restructuring of Nigeria into autonomous regions within a voluntary, inclusive and cooperative federal system based on the consent of the people.” He warned that the historical fears of Nigeria’s minority nationalities must not be ignored. “The fears of minority nationalities were sufficiently serious in the late colonial period to lead to the establishment of the Willink Commission in 1957 to investigate their fears and safeguards. “The Commission acknowledged that many of those fears were justified, although it did not recommend the creation of autonomous regions for the minority areas. “The fact that the minority question has remained unresolved in different forms since then demonstrates an important principle: restructuring must not merely replace one form of domination with another.” According to him, every constituent community must have confidence that its interests would be protected. “If Nigeria is to be restructured into autonomous regions, every constituent community must have confidence that its identity, culture, language, political rights and legitimate economic interests will be protected. “A region should not become a new centre from which one group exercises control or domination over other constituent peoples. “This is why the principle of restructuring by consent is fundamental,” he added. Communities Omololu said the Igbo Leaders of Thought should engage communities they wanted included in their proposed region. His words: “If the Igbo Leaders of Thought believe that particular states or communities should constitute an Igbo Region, we encourage them to engage those states and communities and obtain their freely expressed consent. “Where the people of the proposed constituent areas agree to belong to such a region, and the constitutional requirements for its establishment are satisfied, there should be no controversy arising merely from the identity of the proposed region. “The same principle must apply to every other proposed region. “The South-West does not seek to determine for the people of the South-East, Middle Belt, North, South-South or any other part of Nigeria where they should belong. “Equally, no other group should determine the political identity or regional affiliation of communities in the South-West without their consent.” Omololu said the most important questions were not whether Nigeria should have 10 regions, 17 regions or another number. “The more fundamental questions are: “Who decides? The Citizens or a group of leader? “What do the people concerned want? “Are the proposed boundaries contiguous and viable? “Do the constituent communities freely consent to the arrangement? “What constitutional safeguards will protect minorities within each region?” He said Nigeria’s experience showed that a durable federation must protect both regional autonomy and the rights of constituent communities. “The proposed autonomous regions should consequently be understood as federations of communities, cooperating with one another and with a Federal Government whose powers are limited to those agreed upon by the federating regions,” he submitted. Omololu said the process should not be seen as an attempt to undermine any nationality. “The Concerned Citizens Assembly, we understand is a citizen-centric process and not a project against any nationality. It is an attempt to engage the citizens in creating a constitutional arrangement in which no nationality, region or community needs to fear domination by another. “We therefore welcome dialogue with all groups genuinely committed to restructuring Nigeria. Different proposals should be placed before the Nigerian people, examined openly and negotiated peacefully,” Omololu added. No to democratic vacuum —Adeniran On his part, National Chairman of the Centre for Anti-Corruption and Open Leadership, CACOL, and President of the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights, CDHR, Mr. Debo Adeniran, said the development was significant because it exposed a deeper problem in Nigeria’s restructuring debate. According to him: “There may be growing agreement that the present federal arrangement needs reform, but there is still no consensus on what the replacement should look like. “The rejection by the Igbo Leaders of Thought, ILT, should not simply be dismissed as another ethnic disagreement. “It is a reminder that any attempt to restructure Nigeria must be based on genuine consultation, consensus and the consent of the people concerned.” He warned, however, that restructuring must not become a competition for territorial advantage. “At the same time, every ethnic or regional constituency must recognise that restructuring cannot become a competition for territorial advantage. “The proposal by the ILT for a 10-region structure, including a proposed enlarged Igbo Region extending beyond the five South-East states, inevitably raises questions about boundaries, the wishes of affected communities and the rights of minorities.” Adeniran said such questions must be resolved through transparent processes. “Those questions must be resolved through transparent dialogue and, where necessary, referendums not through historical claims, political pressure or demographic strength.” Election suspension worries Adeniran On the proposal to temporarily suspend the 2027 elections, Adeniran said it was arguably the most consequential aspect of the ILT position. He said: “This proposal deserves serious public debate rather than either immediate endorsement or outright dismissal. “A suspension of elections would have profound constitutional and democratic implications. It would therefore require a clearly defined legal framework, broad national agreement, an explicit timetable, institutional safeguards and mechanisms preventing a transitional arrangement from becoming indefinite.” He warned against creating another governance problem in the process of trying to solve the existing one. “Nigeria must not replace one governance problem with another. Restructuring should deepen democracy, not create a democratic vacuum.” Adeniran also said there was merit in putting fiscal federalism and security architecture at the centre of the national conversation. He said the most important lesson from the disagreement was that Nigeria’s restructuring debate had moved beyond the question of whether restructuring was necessary. “The most important lesson from the disagreement is that Nigeria’s restructuring conversation has finally moved beyond the question of whether restructuring is necessary to the much harder question of what restructuring should actually mean.” ILT is speaking for no one— Ekujumi Giving his perspective, public analyst and human rights advocate, Comrade Nelson Ekujimi, was more dismissive of the ILT position, describing it as an exercise in free speech without a broader mandate. He said: “This Umbrella of Igbo Leaders of Thought, ILT, are merely exercising their fundamental human rights to free speech and to aggregate an opinion on an issue, nothing more, their agitations are mere grandstanding and seeking to excite oneself. “They are free to continue to hallucinate like we always witness groups or organizations indulge in, when elections is knocking on the door, nothing more. “They are speaking for no one, but themselves and their self-interest, Nigerians are not amused by this theatrics from this group.” Differing, President of Yoruba Council Worldwide, His Royal Majesty, Aare Sooko Oladotun Hassan, took a different position, arguing that Nigeria had reached a critical stage where restructuring could no longer be treated as an issue to be postponed whenever elections were approaching. Hassan said: “I strongly believe that Nigeria has reached a critical point in its political history where the question of restructuring can no longer be treated as a matter of political convenience, ethnic bargaining or an issue to be postponed whenever elections are approaching. “The country cannot continue to recycle an unjust and over-centralised federal arrangement and expect a different outcome. What Nigeria needs at this moment is genuine political restructuring that will give every constituent region a sense of belonging, ownership and responsibility in the Nigerian project.” He said the position of the Igbo Leaders of Thought deserved national attention, particularly because of the allegation that the views of the Igbo delegation had not been adequately reflected in the Abuja communiqué. “The position expressed by the Igbo Leaders of Thought on the Abuja restructuring conference communiqué of August 20, 2026, deserves serious national attention. “No meaningful restructuring discussion can be built on exclusion, selective representation or the deliberate disregard of the contributions of any ethnic nationality.” Negotiating table Hassan urged all sides to return to the negotiating table. “If representatives of a major constituent group believe that their position was ignored, the appropriate response should be to return to the negotiating table, address their grievances and build a consensus that genuinely reflects the interests of all Nigerians.” Hassan said Nigeria’s challenge was not its diversity but the manner in which the country had managed its diversity. “I have consistently maintained that Nigeria’s greatest challenge is not its diversity but its failure to manage that diversity through a fair and equitable political structure. “We cannot continue to pretend that the present arrangement is working when insecurity, poverty, unemployment, political instability and the struggle over resources continue to threaten our national cohesion.” On the 10-region proposal, Hassan said it deserved national debate, particularly its proposals for regional control of resources and regional policing. “The proposal for a 10-region political structure, with regional control of resources and regional police, is an idea that deserves open, honest and comprehensive national debate. “The regions must have the authority to develop their economies, harness their natural resources and determine their development priorities without excessive dependence on the Federal Government. “A system in which every region is compelled to look towards Abuja for survival cannot deliver genuine federalism.” Regional policing must have safeguards Hassan also backed decentralised policing but cautioned against abuse. “I am particularly convinced that state and regional policing must become a central component of Nigeria’s security reforms. “It is unreasonable to expect a highly centralised security architecture to effectively address the peculiar security challenges of communities spread across a vast and diverse country. “Those who understand the terrain, culture, language and security dynamics of their communities should have a meaningful role in protecting them, subject to constitutional safeguards, accountability and respect for human rights.” He added: “However, regional policing must not become an instrument of political intimidation or ethnic persecution. “There must be clear constitutional provisions to prevent abuse, protect minorities and guarantee the rights of every Nigerian, irrespective of their ethnic or religious background.” Suspended On the proposal to suspend the 2027 elections, Hassan urged caution, saying restructuring and democracy should not be presented as mutually exclusive. “On the proposal for the temporary suspension of elections until the restructuring exercise is completed, I believe this aspect requires the greatest caution. “Restructuring is urgent, but democracy must not be unnecessarily suspended or used as a bargaining instrument. “Any transition must be founded on constitutional legitimacy, broad national consensus and clearly defined timelines. Nigerians must not be denied their democratic rights under the guise of pursuing a better political arrangement.” He said the approaching elections should not be used as an excuse to abandon the restructuring question. “I do not subscribe to the argument that the 2027 general elections should become an excuse to abandon the restructuring question. “Elections and restructuring must not be presented as mutually exclusive national priorities.” Hassan also cautioned against reducing the restructuring debate to ethnic rivalry. “I also wish to emphasise that restructuring is not an Igbo project, a Yoruba project, a Hausa project or the exclusive ambition of any ethnic nationality. It is a Nigerian project. “The interests of the South-East, South-South, North-Central, North-West, North-East and every other constituent part of Nigeria must equally be recognised. “No ethnic nationality should be made to feel that its future is dependent on the goodwill of another. No region should be permanently disadvantaged by a political arrangement that concentrates power and resources at the centre.” He called on President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the National Assembly, political parties, traditional rulers, socio-cultural organisations and other stakeholders to treat the restructuring debate with urgency. “The Federal Government must provide an inclusive platform where the various positions can be harmonised and translated into actionable constitutional reforms. “The Igbo leaders must also be given the opportunity to fully present their position, just as the Yoruba, Hausa, Middle Belt, Niger Delta and other interest groups must have their voices heard. We cannot build a united country by silencing legitimate disagreements.” Hassan concluded: “My position is simple: Nigeria needs a new and fairer federal compact. “We need a country where the regions can breathe, develop and compete; where security is closer to the people; where resources are managed with responsibility; and where every ethnic nationality has a genuine stake in the federation.” War However, disagreeing with the Igbo leaders, spokesperson for Arewa Consultative Forum, ACF, Prof Tukur Baba, said: “The call for the postponement of the election is not in the constitution. The circumstances under which elections can be postponed, delayed or whatever is clearly stated in the constitution in the case of war or civil unrest and so on and so forth. The constitution clearly states what and how it should be done. The call is therefore not constitutional. We cannot postpone elections. On restructuring, it has nothing to do with the elections with the current structure. The National Assembly has just gone through a process of constitutional changes. Although the details have not been made public, the position of the National Assembly has been transmitted to state assemblies and that is what the constitution says. “None of the state assemblies has come out of the 36 states in the federation. To the best of our knowledge, none of the 36 states have come out to say, this is, this is what I propose, this is our position and so on. We will be shooting in the dark. “For anything to happen, it has to conform to the constitution for now. When the National Assembly started its constitutional review process, the ACF put together a group of experts and we made a comprehensive recommendation to the National Assembly in writing. I remember one of the recommendations we made and I repeat is that certain parts of the constitution should be expunged. For example, the preamble that says, this is one divisible nation, indivisible. We recommended that it should be expunged. “Something related to what the group is calling is that we say, well the constitution should as far as possible make room for any constituent element of the federation that want to secede. They may want to go away and so on. So, but we don’t know whether the recommendation we made has been accepted, rejected or modified. So, we cannot say much about it. But regarding the group itself, the group is not a constitutional group. It has no power to legislate or to dictate. “This is a responsibility for their representatives in the National Assembly. While it is their right and it is the right of every Nigerian to make recommendations on what they think is the way forward for the federation. But this has to be done within what we have the constitutional provisions. “As un-ideal, as defective as they are, this is what we have. “We don’t know that any group, North, West, South and East, has any power to halt elections, to halt the political process or to demand that the federation must be uh restructured in accordance with their wish when and how. “I think it’s a bit arrogant to just come out of a country with 36 states, with over 400 ethnic groups, with various religious followings, with all the diversity that we have for one group to come and hold a brief and hold the nation back on behalf of everyone else. Negotiations “I think if anything is going to be done in the way the group is responding, and it is a non-governmental group, it has to be through negotiation, consultation and give and take within constitutional means. “While they have a right to protest, they have a right to make demands, but these demands have to take into consideration the rights of others. The only way we can do that is through constitutional provision. “I will suggest that the group may wish to take their demand to those states that apply to them, since the state assemblies are making recommendations which will go back to the National Assembly. “I think the right place to go is to go back to the state assemblies and let’s see the way forward from there.” It amounts to selfishness – OPC Meanwhile, speaking on behalf of the Yoruba socio-cultural organisation, Oodua People’s Congress (OPC) Worldwide, its Deputy National Secretary, Otunba Babatunde Thompson, said: “It’s very surprising that some amorphous group, tagging itself Igbo Leaders of Thought, will reject the present framework of six geopolitical developmental regions that is fast becoming accepted and institutionalised in the country’s socio-political environment and has served adequately as the administrative basis for organising the country’s 36 states. “Ironically, recognised Igbo leaders like the Second Republic Vice President, Alex Ekwueme, joined other eminent Nigerians to propose this six-region structure. And their visionary move has indeed helped to settle some fundamental issues relating to the structuring of the country. “Every of the six regions should be in control its own resources, while contributing to the Centre Abuja. This is what the Founder of the Oodua People’s Congress, Dr. Frederick Fasehun clamoured for: restructuring and resource control, and that is the agenda that this present crop of OPC leaders will queue behind. “Moreover, this so-called Igbo Leaders of Thought coming up with the vulgar idea of suspending the 2027 elections amounts to complete selfishness and insensitivity. “We say no in totality to their backward and retrogressive suggestion. “These look like people who don’t believe in their region’s growth and find it very difficult to bring their own region together as one. “However, we shall continue to insist that Nigerians do not yet have a people-created Constitution because the 1999 document we carry today was handed to us by the Military. “The true representatives of Nigerians must come together in a Sovereign National Conference (SNC) to forge an acceptable document that adequately encapsulates the basis of their togetherness as one indivisible nation under God, where no man will be oppressed nor feel oppressed, and where each unit can grow unhindered at its own pace according to its people’s unique aspirations and God-given resources.” The post Abuja declaration: S/West leaders, ACF disagree with Igbo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NAF PLANE CRASH: How hero pilot died saving town
items.description: •He took death to the swamp so we could live — Igbokoda residents •Black box, voice recorder, victims missing seven days after tragedy By Dayo Johnson, Akure It was drizzling in Igbokoda on Monday morning, October 5, 2026. It was the kind of quiet rain that makes fishermen stay indoors and mothers keep their children close.Then the sky screamed. Residents did not first see the aircraft, with tail number NGR 931, carrying 32 people, comprising 25 passengers and seven crew members, on a routine flight from Benin to Lagos. They heard it. A tortured, rattling roar, like metal begging for mercy. “It sounded like the engine was coughing blood,” one fisherman told me at the edge of the swamp. “We looked up and saw it wobbling. It was coming down on our heads.” Where to die Residents said the aircraft was already in trouble long before it crashed. They were unanimous in their belief that, had the pilot not struggled to control it, Igbokoda could have been counting hundreds of dead. “Honestly, the pilot should be commended,” said Jomiloju, a resident. “Many lives would have been lost. It would have been a national tragedy if he had allowed the aircraft to go down in the middle of the community. He struggled with it and brought it down inside a deep swamp, 200 metres away from the town.” Another resident corroborated the account, saying: “If the captain had attempted to bring it down inside the town, it would have caused a bigger disaster. He eventually went into the river and crashed over there.” In Igbokoda, the pilot is no longer just a casualty. He is regarded as a hero. “He is a big hero because he averted a tragedy,” another resident said. “The aircraft was heading towards the community, but he manoeuvred it into the swamp. He should be celebrated in death for saving us from catastrophe. Although we are not happy, 32 persons died. They are family members who paid the ultimate price.” Engine The residents’ account was echoed by Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa when he visited the crash site. According to the governor, eyewitnesses told him that the aircraft came down with a loud sound suggesting engine failure and appeared to be heading towards the town. “But the pilot managed to manoeuvre the aircraft away from the community before it landed about 200 metres away and went straight into the swamp,” Aiyedatiwa said. “Only the pilot, if he had survived, could have explained what happened in those final moments.” What followed was a scene the governor described as “a very gory sight”. When he arrived at the swamp, body parts, military jackets, clothes and fragments of the aircraft were floating on water blackened by aviation fuel. The main fuselage was nowhere to be found. “The aircraft has sunk deep. The nature and depth of the swamp could have caused it to become deeply submerged in the mud,” he said. To reach the wreckage, the state deployed two amphibious excavators, known as swamp buggies, machines designed to float and dig at the same time. Despite the deployment, the main wreckage had yet to be recovered seven days after the crash. Fragments Divers from the Navy and local communities had been searching the swamp, bringing out only fragments of the aircraft. “I saw the divers struggling to locate the main fuselage,” said the Commissioner for Environment, Dr Tob Loko. “One of them said he was able to spot it, but the small boats were insufficient to pull it out. That is why we had to deploy heavier equipment.” The Commissioner for Works, Ayorinde Olawoye, expressed optimism that progress would soon be made. “You can see the swamp buggy is set to float on water and go to where it happened. Within five hours, reasonable progress will be made,” he said. However, the Commissioner for Health, Dr Banji Ajaka, painted a grimmer picture. “It is not something a vehicle or speedboat can just go to. It has gone down with weight and force,” he said. At the site, the Ondo State Commissioner of Police, Felix Ohagwu, who accessed the scene in a canoe, said there were no survivors. “From what we have seen, there are no survivors. What we see is just body parts and clothes littered everywhere, floating in the water,” he said. “It is a very difficult terrain, the creeks, mangroves. Accessing the site was not easy.” Journalists were initially denied access to the site. A television crew was reportedly arrested by Navy personnel for entering without clearance but was later released. Voices For residents, the horror remained fresh. “I was just trying to have my bath when I heard a loud noise. It was very frightening,” Jomiloju recounted. “We rushed towards the direction the sound came from. We had to sail to the location in canoes. All we saw was wreckage. The larger part of the plane was deep inside the swamp.” Another resident, Lucky, added: “We have tried our best to rescue them, but the aircraft was deeply buried inside the swamp. Even the women and men took their canoes.” Where is the black box? Seven days after the crash, critical answers remained trapped in the swamp with the wreckage. The Nigerian Air Force confirmed that the flight data recorder, commonly referred to as the black box, and the cockpit voice recorder had yet to be recovered. “We hope to be able to find critical components of the aircraft that will speak to the investigators because the aircraft wreckage actually speaks to the investigators,” Air Vice Marshal Ebimobo Ebiowe, NAF Superintendent of Standards and Evaluation, said at the site. Investigation The Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, who visited Igbokoda and inspected the site, ordered a high-level investigation involving military and civilian aviation safety experts, the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau and retired senior officers. “I have flown on this aeroplane. My family has flown on this aeroplane. I know each of the crew personally. They are highly trained, professional and intelligent officers. The best we can do is to honour the sacrifice they have made,” Aneke said, appealing to Nigerians to avoid speculation. Governor Aiyedatiwa described the incident as a national tragedy, commiserating with President Bola Tinubu, the Nigerian Air Force and the families of the personnel who died while in active service. Scan sonar As of Saturday, the Navy had deployed side-scan sonar equipment to map the swamp and locate the submerged fuselage. Aviation fuel was also reported to be leaking into the water, raising concerns about pollution. In Igbokoda, two tragedies are being mourned: the 32 lives lost in the swamp and the potentially greater tragedy that residents believe was averted by a pilot who, in his final moments, steered the aircraft away from the town. Whenever it drizzles on a Monday morning, they will remember the day the sky screamed and a man, in their eyes, chose where to die. The post NAF PLANE CRASH: How hero pilot died saving town appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Banques : le besoin de liquidité se creuse à 136,5 MMDH en septembre
items.description: Le besoin de liquidité bancaire s’est creusé à 136,5 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) en moyenne hebdomadaire en septembre 2026, contre 133,1 MMDH un mois auparavant, ressort-il de la récente Revue mensuelle de la conjoncture économique, monétaire et financière de Bank Al-Maghrib (BAM). Dans ce contexte, BAM a ramené le volume global de ses injections à 152,5 MMDH, réparti entre 57,1 MMDH sous forme d’avances à 7 jours, 47,6 MMDH au titre des opérations de pension livrée à 1 et 3 mois et 47,8 MMDH destinés au refinancement via les prêts garantis à long terme. Au niveau du marché interbancaire, le volume quotidien moyen des échanges s’est situé à 3,9 MMDH et le taux moyen pondéré s’est établi à 2,25%, fait savoir la même source. Sur le marché des bons du Trésor, les taux sont restés globalement quasi-stables en août aussi bien sur le marché primaire que secondaire. Quant aux taux créditeurs appliqués aux dépôts bancaires, ils ont enregistré en août un recul mensuel de 30 points de base (pb) à 2,15% pour ceux à 6 mois et une augmentation de 7 pb à 2,65% pour ceux à un an. Pour ce qui est du taux minimum de rémunération des comptes sur carnet, il a été fixé pour le deuxième semestre de l’année 2026 à 1,82%, en hausse de 21 pb par rapport au semestre précédent. En parallèle, les résultats de l’enquête de Bank Al-Maghrib auprès des banques relatifs au deuxième trimestre de 2026, font ressortir une augmentation trimestrielle de 15 pb du taux moyen global à 4,81%. Par secteur institutionnel, les taux assortissant les crédits aux entreprises non financières ont augmenté de 17 pb à 4,71%, traduisant des hausses de 29 pb à 4,65% pour les prêts à l’équipement et de 16 pb à 4,62% pour les facilités de trésorerie, ainsi qu’une baisse de 2 pb à 5,35% pour les crédits à la promotion immobilière. Par taille d’entreprises, les taux sont restés quasi stables à 4,56% pour les grandes entreprises et à 5,2% pour les TPME. Concernant les taux appliqués aux particuliers, ils ont baissé de 15 pb à 5,59%, avec des replis de 170 pb à 5,51% pour les comptes débiteurs et crédits de trésorerie, de 13 pb à 4,53% pour ceux à l’habitat et de 5 pb à 6,81% pour ceux à la consommation. The post Banques : le besoin de liquidité se creuse à 136,5 MMDH en septembre appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : Youssou Ndour associé à la promotion des Jeux à Paris
items.description: Les Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026 poursuivent leur campagne de promotion à l’international. À l’occasion du Grand Bal de Youssou Ndour, prévu à Bercy, à Paris, la mascotte officielle des Jeux, Ayo, fera le déplacement pour porter les couleurs de cet événement historique pour le sport africain. La présence d’Ayo sur la scène de Bercy constituera une occasion de mettre en lumière Dakar 2026 auprès du public parisien et de la diaspora sénégalaise. À travers cette initiative, les organisateurs entendent profiter de la portée du rendez-vous musical de Youssou Ndour pour renforcer la visibilité des Jeux et susciter l’intérêt autour de cette compétition internationale. Prévu à Dakar en 2026 du 31 octobre au 13 novemvre entre Dakar, Saly et Diamniadio, cet événement revêt une dimension particulière puisqu’il s’agira de la première édition des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse organisée sur le continent africain. L’association de la musique, de la culture et du sport s’inscrit ainsi dans une dynamique de rayonnement international du Sénégal et de promotion de son rendez-vous olympique. En investissant la scène de Bercy, Ayo contribuera à faire connaître davantage Dakar 2026, tout en portant un message d’ouverture et de célébration de la jeunesse à travers le sport. C.G.D

items.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens to category 4 as it nears western Mexico
items.description: Hurricane Simon strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm as it swept toward Mexico's west coast, where it was expected to make landfall late Saturday or early Sunday. The US National Hurricane Center said Simon could strengthen further as it approaches west-central Mexico with winds of 240 kilometers per hour. "Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion shortly in the hurricane warning area," the center said. As Florida assessed the damage caused by Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Mexico braced for Simon. Simon is the latest in a busy hurricane season in the Pacific, where the powerful El Nino ocean-warming phenomenon is weakening wind shear, allowing storms to gain strength. In the Pacific tourist resort of Puerto Vallarta, the skies were cloudy on Saturday morning, but the sea was still relatively calm. Torrential rains caused by Simon have already caused flooding in Acapulco, another major tourist destination farther south. But residents of Puerto Vallarta, which sits on a huge horseshoe-shaped bay that helps defuse the power of a hurricane, appeared largely unfazed by the threat. While shop owners sandbagged the entrances to their stores and boarded up the doors and windows, there was little sense of impending disaster. "Simon says: 'Everything is going to be alright,'" someone had spray-painted on a board, in a play on the name of a popular children's game. Moises Villasenor, 72, said he was "a little worried" as he filled sandbags to protect his small hotel, about three blocks from the seafront. But, on the whole, he said, "We're very positive." Tourists also exuded calm. "We're going to enjoy it as much as we can, even if it's just for today," said Edna Morales, 41, who arrived on Friday from northern Mexico with her husband to celebrate their wedding anniversary. Authorities said they would order residents to take shelter starting at 5:00 p.m. (2300 GMT)

items.title: Power restoration fault suspected in Kumasi Central Market fire
items.description: The Ghana National Fire Service is investigating a suspected power-restoration fault as a possible trigger for a fire that swept through part of the Kumasi Central Market near the Aboabo station. Ashanti Regional Fire Commander ACFO I Peter Tetteh said preliminary eyewitness accounts indicated that the fire started shortly after electricity returned following a brief outage. He disclosed this during an inspection of the fire-ravaged area with the Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, Ashanti Regional Minister Dr Frank Amoakohene and Kumasi Mayor Richard Ofori Agyemang Boadi. “From what we heard, eyewitnesses said there was a light out. In three minutes, the light came back on, and that is when they saw the fire,” he said. The account has not yet been established as the definitive cause of the outbreak, with investigations still ongoing. Mr Tetteh said traders who had received basic fire safety training attempted to put out the initial flames using portable fire extinguishers before firefighters arrived. Their efforts, however, were overtaken by the rapid spread of the fire. He said the first fire appliance from Asokore Mampong arrived at the scene at 8:39 pm, after which crews established containment lines to prevent the flames from spreading to other sections of the market. A total of five appliances were deployed, comprising four fire tenders and one water tanker. “We didn’t have a problem with water at all yesterday,” Mr Tetteh said, indicating that water supply was not a constraint during the operation. Despite the available water supply and police presence, the Fire Commander said congestion and obstructions caused by traders trying to retrieve their belongings made it difficult for crews to manoeuvre around the market. He said the conditions complicated efforts to access affected areas and contain the blaze. “There were a lot of obstructions yesterday. Even the police were here, but it was very, very difficult over here,” he said. Investigations into the precise cause of the fire and assessments of the total financial losses are continuing.

items.title: Le libre-échange séduit les Marocains, la ZLECAf reste peu connue
items.description: Les Marocains affichent une forte adhésion au libre-échange et aux échanges avec les marchés internationaux. En revanche, la Zone de libre-échange continentale africaine, pourtant au cœur de la stratégie d'intégration économique du continent, demeure largement méconnue du grand public, selon le « African insights 2026 » d'Afrobarometer. Le Maroc apparaît comme l'un des pays africains les plus favorables à l'ouverture commerciale, mais aussi comme l'un de ceux où la principale initiative d'intégration économique du continent demeure largement méconnue. C'est l'un des principaux enseignements de « African insights 2026 » d'Afrobarometer, consacré à la perception des Africains face aux mutations de l'ordre mondial. Réalisée dans 38 pays africains, l'enquête met en lumière un contraste entre les orientations stratégiques défendues par les États et leur appropriation par les citoyens. Le cas du Maroc illustre particulièrement ce décalage. Une adhésion nette au libre-échange Selon l'étude, 65% des Marocains estiment qu'il est préférable pour l'économie nationale que le gouvernement facilite les échanges commerciaux avec les autres pays afin de créer davantage d'opportunités économiques. À l'inverse, seuls 25% privilégient une politique consistant à limiter les échanges afin de protéger les producteurs locaux. Ce niveau de soutien dépasse la moyenne continentale, établie à 62%, et place le Maroc parmi les pays d'Afrique du Nord les plus favorables au libre-échange. Pour Afrobarometer, cette tendance s'inscrit dans un mouvement plus large observé à l'échelle du continent. Alors que les discours protectionnistes gagnent du terrain dans plusieurs régions du monde, les Africains demeurent majoritairement convaincus des bénéfices de l'ouverture commerciale. Une préférence assumée pour les marchés mondiaux L'étude montre également que les Marocains privilégient clairement une stratégie commerciale tournée vers l'international. Interrogés sur les partenaires avec lesquels leur gouvernement devrait développer les échanges, 72% répondent que le Maroc devrait renforcer ses relations commerciales avec l'ensemble du monde. Seuls 18% estiment que la priorité devrait être donnée aux autres pays africains, tandis que 10% privilégient les partenaires du voisinage régional. Ce résultat figure parmi les plus élevés du continent et reflète une vision largement ouverte des débouchés commerciaux, bien au-delà du seul espace africain. La ZLECAf reste largement méconnue Cette forte adhésion au principe du libre-échange contraste toutefois avec la très faible notoriété de la Zone de libre-échange continentale africaine. À peine 6% des Marocains déclarent avoir entendu parler de la ZLECAf, tandis que 94% indiquent ne pas connaître cet accord, pourtant présenté comme le principal projet économique de l'Union africaine. Ce constat illustre l'écart entre les ambitions institutionnelles et leur diffusion auprès des citoyens. Afrobarometer souligne d'ailleurs que cette méconnaissance constitue un phénomène continental : en moyenne, seuls 13% des Africains disent connaître l'existence de la ZLECAf. Le rapport estime que les gouvernements devront renforcer leurs efforts de communication s'ils souhaitent obtenir une véritable adhésion populaire à cette initiative d'intégration économique. Une ouverture également sur la circulation des personnes L'enquête révèle enfin que cette ouverture ne se limite pas aux échanges commerciaux. Au Maroc, 63% des personnes interrogées se déclarent favorables à la libre circulation des personnes entre les pays africains, contre 38% qui souhaitent davantage de restrictions afin de protéger les emplois et les opportunités économiques nationales. Là encore, le Royaume se situe au-dessus de la moyenne continentale, fixée à 56%. Le rapport dresse ainsi le portrait d'une opinion publique marocaine largement favorable à l'ouverture économique et aux échanges internationaux. Il met toutefois en évidence un déficit de connaissance des principaux instruments d'intégration africaine, à commencer par la ZLECAf, pourtant appelée à jouer un rôle central dans le développement du commerce intra-africain au cours des prochaines années. The post Le libre-échange séduit les Marocains, la ZLECAf reste peu connue appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Le nouveau gouvernement de Moctar O. Diay : Dix départs dont trois ministres de souveraineté
items.description: Dix ministres ont quitté le nouveau gouvernement mauritanien, dont la composition a été annoncée ce samedi, après la reconduction de Mokhtar Ould Diay au poste de Premier ministre et sa mission de former un nouveau gouvernement. Les changements ont concerné les ministères de la Défense, de l’Intérieur, de l’Énergie, des Affaires islamiques, de la Culture, des Affaires économiques et du développement, ainsi que l’élevage, sans oublier le Secrétariat général du gouvernement. Hanane Ould Sidi a quitté le ministère de la Défense, chargé des retraités et des enfants de martyrs, après sept ans à ce poste ; il est remplacé par Ba Ousmane. Mohamed Ahmed Ould Mohamed Lemine a également quitté le ministère de l’Intérieur, de la Décentralisation et du Développement local, à la tête duquel il avait été nommé en mars 2022, après avoir occupé auparavant le poste de directeur du cabinet du président de la République ; il est remplacé par Mokhtar Ould Ahmed Bouceif. Au ministère de l’Énergie et du Pétrole, Mohamed Abdel Fattah a succédé à l’ancien ministre Mohamed Khaled, nommé à ce poste en 2024 et dont le nom avait été cité dans l’enquête relative aux incendies liés au réseau électrique. Al-Vadl Ould Sidati Ould Ahmed Louli a quitté le ministère des Affaires islamiques et de l’enseignement originel, après avoir précédemment occupé le portefeuille de la Pêche remplacé par Sayed ElHaj Ould Dah. Houssein Ould Medou a également quitté le ministère de la Culture, des Arts, de la Communication et des Relations avec le Parlement, à la tête duquel il avait été nommé en 2024 ; il occupait également le poste de porte-parole du gouvernement. Il a été remplacé par Mohamed Babana. Parmi les départs figuraient également Mokhtar ElHusseinou Lam, ministre chargé du Secrétariat général du gouvernement, auquel a succédé Mokhtar Abdallahi, ainsi qu’Abdallahi Souleymane Ould Cheikh Sidiya, qui a quitté le ministère des Affaires économiques et du Développement après avoir rejoint le gouvernement lors d’un remaniement ministériel effectué l’année dernière ; il a été remplacé par Mohamedou Ould M’Haimid. Sidi Ahmed Ould Mohamed a quitté le ministère de l'élevage, où il a été remplacé par Ahmedit Ould El-Chine. Au niveau de la présidence de la République, Moulay Ould Mohamed Laghdaf a quitté ses fonctions de ministre secrétaire général de la présidence ; il a été remplacé par Aïssata Ba Yahya, qui occupait auparavant le poste de ministre conseillère à la présidence de la République.

items.title: Mamou : trois affaires impliquant des enfants alertent les familles
items.description: La ville de Mamou a été confrontée à trois incidents impliquant des enfants entre le 9 et le 10 octobre 2026. Entre une tentative présumée d’enlèvement à Telico, l’abandon d’un nouveau-né à Kimbely 2 et la sortie nocturne d’une fillette de trois ans à Hamdalaye, ces événements suscitent de vives préoccupations autour de la protection des enfants. À Telico, l'enfant du chef de quartier âgé de deux ans échappe à un enlèvement Les faits se sont déroulés aux environs de 4 heures du matin, le vendredi 9 octobre, dans la commune urbaine de Mamou. Un individu inconnu a profité de la sortie de la mère pour se mettre à l'aise pour pénétrer dans la maison et emporter un enfant de deux ans qui dormait dans son lit. En apercevant l’individu avec son enfant, la mère a immédiatement crié au secours et s’est lancée à sa poursuite. Pris dans cette situation, le suspect a abandonné le petit derrière la cour avant de prendre la fuite. Le père de l’enfant, Thierno Ibrahima Sory Sow, témoigne : « Lorsque ma femme a aperçu l’individu disparaître avec l’enfant, elle a crié au secours et l’a poursuivi en criant. L’individu a abandonné l’enfant derrière la cour avant de prendre la poudre d’escampette . » L’enfant a ainsi été retrouvé sain et sauf, évitant une issue qui aurait pu être dramatique pour sa famille. À Kimbely 2, un nouveau-né abandonné dans la végétation Le même vendredi, une autre situation préoccupante a été signalée au quartier Kimbely 2. Un nouveau-né de sexe masculin a été découvert dans des herbes, derrière une concession. La femme soupçonnée de l’avoir abandonné a disparu. Alerté, le chef de quartier, Mamadou Macka Barry, a immédiatement informé la mairie. Les autorités concernées, accompagnées notamment des agents de la Protection civile, se sont rendues sur les lieux avant l’évacuation du nourrisson à l’hôpital de Mamou. D’après son témoignage, le cordon ombilical du bébé était mal coupé et le nourrisson, enveloppé dans un pull-over, souffrait du froid. Le chef de quartier indique avoir mobilisé des vêtements pour le bébé, tandis que la Direction préfectorale de l’action sociale s’est engagée à trouver une solution pour son alimentation. Le nouveau-né est actuellement pris en charge au service de pédiatrie de l’hôpital de Mamou. Pendant ce temps, sa mère présumée est activement recherchée. À Hamdalaye, une fillette de trois ans, disparue pendant la nuit, retrouvée à la gendarmerie Dans la nuit du vendredi au samedi 10 octobre, une autre scène d’inquiétude s’est produite à Hamdalaye, dans le quartier Saabou. Une fillette de trois ans a quitté la concession familiale pendant que tout le monde dormait. Selon son père, Ibrahima Sow, l’enfant se serait réveillée aux environs de 2 heures du matin avant d’ouvrir la porte du couloir et de sortir sans être remarquée. C’est vers 4 heures que le père a constaté son absence. Après des recherches infructueuses dans la maison et le voisinage, il a alerté les forces de sécurité. « Je me suis réveillé à 4 heures. Après la toilette, j’ai remarqué que la fillette n’était plus à sa place. J’ai fouillé dans la maison et constaté que la porte du couloir était ouverte. Nous avons recherché l’enfant partout, en vain. C’est ainsi que j’ai saisi la gendarmerie et la police », raconte-t-il. Le père sera finalement informé que sa fille se trouve à la gendarmerie. D’après les explications qui lui ont été fournies, la fillette aurait parcouru une centaine de mètres avant de rencontrer un individu près d’un terrain de football, aux environs de 2 h 45. Elle lui aurait dit qu’elle se rendait à l’école. L’homme l’aurait ensuite conduite chez un médecin installé à proximité. Au cours de la matinée, le médecin aurait amené l’enfant à la gendarmerie, où son père a pu la retrouver. Ces trois événements, survenus en l’espace de quelques heures dans différents quartiers de Mamou, rappellent les risques auxquels les enfants en bas âge peuvent être exposés.

items.title: The 7-foot giant of Ngleshie Amanfro: Seven-foot Ghanaian Ephraim Saawa dreams of joining the national basketball team
items.description: In Ngleshie Amanfro, a bustling community in the Ga South Municipality, you don’t need to know his name to know him. You just look up. At 7.0 feet tall, Ephraim Sincero Ma-c Saawa is impossible to miss. Trotro mates call him to the front seat. Children stop and stare. Adults pull out their phones for a quick picture. Strangers on the streets from Amanfro through to Kasoa stop him to ask the same question: “How tall are you?” For many, that attention would be a burden. For Ephraim, it could be a destiny he cannot do away with. The young Senior High School graduate wants to turn the curious looks into cheers in a basketball arena. His ultimate dream is simple but audacious: to wear the red, gold and green of Ghana, step onto the international basketball court, and bring home a trophy for his country. “I want to join Ghana’s national basketball team, compete in international tournaments and help win a trophy for the country,” he told MyJoyOnline in an interview that captures both his humility and his hunger. Ephraim is not yet a household name in Ghanaian sports. He has no national caps, no league titles, no endorsement deals. But in Ngleshie Amanfro, he is already a local celebrity — the towering pride of the community whose physical gift many believe could become Ghana’s sporting advantage. He comes from Nandom Piina in the Upper West Region, but his story is taking shape in Greater Accra. He completed Abakrampa Senior High School in 2025 in the Central Region, where he studied Business. While his mates were focused on football — the default passion in almost every Ghanaian second cycle school — Ephraim’s eyes were on the basket. It was not always basketball. At basic school, he was a volleyball player. His height made him natural at the net. But by the time he got to Senior High School, his heart had switched courts. “By the time I reached senior high school, my dream was to play basketball rather than volleyball,” he recalled. The problem was that his school had no basketball court. While Abakrampa SHS chalked up successes in athletics and football, basketball was a sport played in his imagination and wherever he could find students from other schools to train with. “First, I need to learn to play basketball very well. That way, if I get the opportunity to join the national team, I will be able to perform well and help the team,” he said — a statement that shows he understands that height alone does not make a baller. That structured learning has now begun. For the past two months, Ephraim has been training with the Magic Basket Ball Academy, based at Tudu close to the Accra Technical University. The opportunity came through his father, who refused to let his son’s potential go to waste. “My father took me to meet the coach and spoke to him about training me,” he explained. At Magic, he is learning to convert his natural attributes the long legs that power high vertical jumps for rebounds, the long strides that allow quick first steps for drives to the basket into real basketball Footwork, positioning, shooting, and defending. His role model is no surprise: French phenomenon Victor Wembanyama, the 7-foot-4-inch NBA superstar who has redefined what a big man can do. Ephraim does not just admire Wembanyama’s height; he admires how he uses it.”I admire how he plays, especially his defensive skills. That is why he is my role model,” he said. He points to Wembanyama’s shot-blocking, his rebounding dominance, and his selfless support for teammates as the blueprint he wants to follow. So strong is his admiration that he openly appeals for a chance to meet Wembanyama one day, mentioning Ghanaian businessman Ibrahim Mahama as someone he hopes could help make that dream encounter possible. For now, he is willing to join any professional team that will give him a chance to learn, to grow, and to contribute to winning tournaments and league titles. A Celebrity Without Trying. His challenge is how to get good training kits. Away from the court, Ephraim’s life is a lesson in living tall literally and figuratively — in a world built for average height. He says the fascination with his height started as early as basic school. Teachers and pupils alike were amazed. At Abakrampa SHS, he was officially the tallest student on campus. Today, a simple walk to buy something in Ngleshie Amanfro becomes a meet-and-greet.”Some people laugh, while others are surprised. Some approach me to take pictures or ask for my phone number, and we become friends,” he said with a smile. Many in the community now call him the tallest boy in Accra, but he is quick to deflect the title with disarming humility. “I cannot say that because I have not seen everyone in Accra. I believe there may be people who are taller than me,” he said. But the fame has its frustrations, especially with transportation. Ghana’s ubiquitous trotros were not designed with 7-foot passengers in mind. “If I sit at the back, I sometimes experience leg pain by the time I reach my destination. That is why I usually sit in front,” he explained. It has become a daily negotiation. If the front seat is taken, he politely asks the driver’s mate to intervene and explain his condition to the occupant. Some passengers understand and swap seats. Others refuse, and Ephraim simply waits for the next car. He wants public transport to be more accommodating and for drivers and mates to be more empathetic for people like him and others. “They should explain our difficulties to other passengers so that people understand why sitting at the back can be uncomfortable for us,” he appealed. Beyond The Court: Coding And Community. What makes Ephraim’s story compelling is that basketball is only one half of his ambition. While he works at a printing press in Ngleshie Amanfro to make ends meet, he is preparing to pursue university education in Computer Science. He wants to become a software engineer. His motivation is not just personal advancement. He is worried about how young Ghanaians are using technology. He says he has seen many students rely completely on Artificial Intelligence to do assignments without actually learning. “I would like to create software that helps children and young people understand the world better and respond to what is happening around them,” he said. He also dreams of establishing small businesses to support himself and his family. More importantly, he wants to turn his visibility into a vehicle for positive change. In a community where many young people are at risk of falling into gangs and social vices, he believes his towering presence can carry a towering message. “I would like to encourage them to focus on their lives and their future rather than engage in social vices,” he said. From the streets of Amanfro where he is stopped for selfies, to the dusty court at Tudu where he is learning to block and rebound, to the printing press where he works and the future computer lab where he hopes to code, Ephraim Sincero Ma-c Saawa is walking — tall — towards two futures at once. One is in Silicon Valley-inspired dreams of software that educates Ghanaian children. The other is in a Ghana jersey, hearing the national anthem before a big game, ready to jump for the opening tip-off. For Ghana basketball, which has long searched for its next big man to compete with Nigeria, Senegal and Angola on the continent, the giant of Ngleshie Amanfro might just be worth a look.

items.title: Government promises support for Kumasi Central Market fire victims
items.description: The government has assured traders affected by a fire at Kumasi Central Market of possible state support, with the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) expected to assess the damage and determine the assistance required. Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs Mahama Ayariga gave the assurance during an emergency visit to the scene with Ashanti Regional Minister Dr Frank Amoakohene and Kumasi Mayor Richard Ofori Agyemang Boadi. The visit followed a directive from the President to assess the situation after the blaze destroyed 15 shops before being contained by firefighters. Addressing affected traders, Mr Ayariga conveyed the President’s sympathies and said the government would consider available options to help them recover from their losses. “We will put our heads together to see how we can lift you out of this unfortunate situation,” he said. “When we get the report from NADMO, we will explore every opportunity that exists to support the victims.” Mr Ayariga said the government, in coordination with the Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly (KMA), had agreed to allow affected shop owners to temporarily restore their trading spaces ahead of the Christmas season, provided the areas meet structural safety requirements. KMA engineers are to conduct urgent structural integrity tests on the affected sections before traders can return to their shops. The assessment is expected to help determine whether the affected spaces can safely accommodate trading activities while relief arrangements are considered. The Minister also announced that construction works on Phase Two of the Kejetia Market project, which have stalled, would resume shortly. He said the project was intended to help address market congestion, although no specific date for the resumption was provided in the statement. The proposed restart comes as traders and authorities assess the impact of the latest fire and consider measures to restore affected businesses ahead of the busy Christmas trading period.
